objectives: Explain the chapter’s definition of a Sufi and present the outer and inner norms as two complementary sides of one lifestyle.

Evaluate the two fields in which the chapter presents Yunus as important (Sufi life and the development of literary Turkish) and the link the text itself makes between them (“a literary tradition based on Sufism”).

Discover what “whereas” does, how a second role is added (In addition, … / In addition to + -ing) and why a preposition is followed by an -ing form (the pursuit of becoming, without expecting any return).
Keep the scope of importance claims (“one of the first”, “a significant contribution”) instead of upgrading them.
content.pedagogy: Open with the question “Two sides or two choices?” Learners read the whereas-sentence together with the sentence before it and must prove, with a quotation, whether a Sufi keeps both sides. Pairs then build a two-field identity map (Sufi life / literary Turkish) and draw a link only where the text supports one. The grammar is discovered: Learners explain what whereas does before you name it, and they formulate the preposition + -ing rule from the principles sentence before you confirm it.
priorKnowledge: Relative clauses (a person who …), gerunds after common prepositions (good at -ing), and the difference between a definition and an evaluation.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “Whereas” does not mean the inner side replaces the outer side; the previous sentence says Sufis live within both.
The chapter says Yunus was “one of the first” and “one of the Turkish poets” with a crucial role; learners should not upgrade this to “the first” or “the only”.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: whereas for two different but complementary sides · adding a second role (In addition, / Moreover, + new sentence · In addition to + noun or -ing) · preposition + -ing (the pursuit of becoming better people, without expecting any return).
Notice (Activity 1): Board “The outer part relates to the body’s acts of worship, whereas the inner side handles the morality and intentions of the heart.” together with “Sufis maintain a lifestyle within the outer (visible) and inner norms of Islam.” Ask: “Does a Sufi choose one side or keep both? Which sentence tells you?” Learners say what whereas does (two sides compared, not replacement, not time order) before you confirm it.
Build (Activities 2–3): Add the second identity in two ways (In addition, he was one of the first … / In addition to being one of the first …, he played a crucial role …), then repair “of become” and “without expect”. Learners state the rule themselves: After a preposition, a noun or an -ing form.
Likely errors: *In addition to be one of the first · *In addition, to his standing … (mixing the adverb and the preposition) · *without expect / *without to expect · *the pursuit of become · whereas used for a sequence in time.
Use (Activity 4): 6–8 sentences explaining how the chapter presents Yunus as important in two different but connected fields, with one whereas-sentence, one “in addition to + -ing” and one preposition + -ing, then two sentences about a person learners know who is important in two fields.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Chunk the definition into three meaning units: “a SUfi is a PERson | who SEEKS CLOSEness to alLAH | by aDOPTing ISlamic MYSticism”.
Contrastive stress around whereas, with a short pause before it: “the OUTer part relates to the BOdy’s acts of WORship, | whereAS the INner side …”.
The list of principles: A slight rise on each item and a fall on the last: “… such as WEALTH↗, STAtus↗, and FAME↘”; “of” and “to” stay weak (/əv/, /tə/).
-ing endings are clear but unstressed: BEcoming, GIVing, exPECTing, DOing, atTACHing.
Word focus: MYS-ti-cism, CRU-cial, mo-RAL-i-ty, PREJ-u-dice, pos-SES-sions, con-tri-BU-tion.
beforeReading: Write two headings on the board: “What people can see” / “What only the heart knows”. Pairs place three ideas (praying, an honest intention, giving to charity) and discuss whether one religious life can include both. Keep the answers as hypotheses to test against the text.
duringReading: First listening, books closed: In how many fields is Yunus important?
Box the definition of a Sufi and underline the sentence that says Sufis live within both outer and inner norms.
Number the six moral principles and circle the one with a condition (without expecting any return).
In paragraph 2, underline every phrase that shows importance and rank its strength (one of the first, crucial, significant, one of the most important factors).
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the definition and the two-field map in view.

Language Focus: Discover what whereas does (Activity 1), add a second identity in two ways (Activity 2), repair the preposition + -ing forms (Activity 3), then write the two-field analysis (Activity 4).
Transfer: Describe a person in your community who is important in two connected fields, keeping the scope of every claim (one of …, a significant …).
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: Pairs sort praying / an honest intention / giving to charity under “What people can see” and “What only the heart knows”, two pairs report; 4–11 Listen with books closed (in how many fields is Yunus important?), then read along and box the definition; 11–18 Two-field identity map in pairs: Sufi life / literary Turkish, every branch with a quoted phrase, then the class agrees on the one link the text supports (“a literary tradition based on Sufism”); 18–21 Quick Challenge individually; 21–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Does a Sufi choose one side or keep both?), Activities 2–3 in pairs, learners state the preposition + -ing rule before you confirm it; 31–38 Use: Activity 4 in 6–8 sentences, partners check that no “one of the first” has become “the first”; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why does the writer use whereas and not instead or but to describe the outer and inner norms?
What does “without expecting any return” add to “giving generously”? Is giving still generous if you expect something back?
Which is the stronger claim: “one of the first to create and perform poetry … in plain Turkish” or “the first”? Why does the difference matter?
How does the chapter connect Yunus’s Sufi identity with his literary role?
interactiveTips: Use the Outer and Inner hotspot after learners have boxed the definition, to confirm the outer/inner distinction.
Use the Plain Turkish hotspot when learners discuss his contribution to literary Turkish.
Replay the moral-principles sentence and ask learners to count the -ing forms they hear.
Do not expand the definition of Sufism with outside doctrinal detail.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the frame “The outer part relates to ____, whereas the inner side ____. In addition to being ____, Yunus Emre ____.” Let learners first copy the preposition + -ing phrases from the text into two columns (preposition / -ing form).
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write 8–10 sentences evaluating which of Yunus’s two roles the chapter emphasises more, using whereas, in addition to + -ing and one hedged claim (arguably, one of the …), with two quoted phrases as evidence.

formativeAssessment: Explains whereas as a contrast between two complementary sides, using the previous sentence as evidence.
Uses a preposition + -ing accurately in new sentences.
Keeps the scope of importance claims.
expectedResponses: A Sufi seeks closeness to Allah by adopting Islamic mysticism and lives within both the outer and the inner norms of Islam; in addition to being a Sufi, Yunus was one of the first to create and perform poetry in plain Turkish and made a significant contribution to Turkish as a literary language.
content.transferTask: Describe someone in your community who is important in two connected fields, using whereas and in addition to + -ing, without exaggerating their role.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners work out the function of whereas from the text before I named it, and did they keep “one of the first” from turning into “the first”?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, make a two-field identity map: Sufi life and literary Turkish. Put a quoted phrase on every branch. Then the class agrees on the one link the text supports.
checkQuestions: What are the two fields? (Sufi life, literary Turkish)
How many links do we agree on? (one, the link the text supports)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that the definition is taken from the box. In Activity 1, ask what the previous sentence shows about whereas. In the Use task, check that claims about importance keep their scope, such as one of the first.

exitTicket: Write one whereas-sentence about two sides of school life and one sentence with “without + -ing”.

rubricLevels.secure: Defines a Sufi accurately from the text.
Explains whereas as a contrast between two sides that complete each other.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Do the two sides cancel each other?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses in addition to and a preposition + -ing accurately.
Keeps the scope of claims, such as one of the first.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “The first, or one of the first?”.

interculturalFocus.notice: Yunus is presented as important in Sufi life and in the development of literary Turkish, and the chapter describes giving generously 'without expecting any return'.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Which English and Turkish words describe giving without expecting anything back ('selfless', 'altruism'; 'karşılıksız', 'diğergâmlık')? Is there a custom in Türkiye such as 'askıda ekmek' and in English-speaking countries such as 'pay it forward'?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners describe generosity customs from several cultures without ranking them.

objectives: Evaluate the claim that Yunus’s style is balanced and explain how “Thus” turns it into a result (literary value and easy to understand).
Grade biographical claims by certainty: Attributed (According to historical accounts), generally accepted (the widely accepted view, is considered), partial (Some sources note) or stated directly.
Discover how neither … nor, both … and and not limited to shape the picture of his style and education.
Explain the double role of tekkes (Sufi training and civil society organisations) without generalising beyond the chapter.
content.pedagogy: Run a certainty audit. Groups grade every biographical sentence on a four-step scale (stated / widely accepted / attributed / some sources) and must name the words that justify each grade. The language work grows out of this: Learners discover that the writer’s hedges are part of the information, and then that neither … nor rejects two extremes while “not limited to” widens a claim. Let learners argue borderline cases (Is “He is considered the founder” certain?) instead of settling them yourself.
priorKnowledge: Both … and; simple reporting (people say that …); the difference between a fact and an opinion.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “The widely accepted view” is not proof and “some sources” are not all sources; 1240–41 and 1320–21 are approximate ranges.
“Not limited to madrasas” does not mean he did not study at a madrasa; it widens his education to the tekke.
Plain style is not weak style: The chapter says his works have literary value.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: source stance and certainty (According to historical accounts, … · According to the widely accepted view, … · He is considered … · Some sources note that …) · neither … nor … for rejecting two extremes · both … and … for two qualities at once · not limited to … also … for widening the scope.
Notice (Activities 1–2): learners sort six chapter sentences into “the writer reports or qualifies the claim” / “the writer states it directly”. Ask: “Which words show the writer is not fully sure? Why would a writer be careful about a poet who lived in the 13th century?” Then they choose the rewrite that keeps the certainty of “the widely accepted view” (Most scholars accept that …).
Build (Activity 3): Complete “His style is neither too simple nor too complex. Thus, his works both have literary value and are easy to understand. … However, his education was not limited to madrasas.” and explain why either … or would change the meaning.
Likely errors: *neither too simple or too complex · *either too simple nor · *According historical accounts · *Some sources notes · *not limited in madrasas · certainty upgraded (It is proven that …).
Use (Activity 4): Summarise Yunus’s education in 5–7 sentences without making uncertain details sound certain, then write two hedged sentences about another historical figure.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Balanced contrast with stress on the two extremes: “NEIther too SIMple | nor too COMplex”, then a clear pause before “THUS, |”.
Source frames as single units followed by a pause: “acCORDing to hisTORical acCOUNTS, | …”, “some SOURces NOTE that | …”.
Dates as ranges: “twelve forty to twelve forty-one”, “thirteen twenty to thirteen twenty-one”.
Word focus: con-TEM-po-rar-y, phi-LOS-o-phy, fun-da-MEN-tal, sol-i-DAR-i-ty, co-op-er-A-tion, MAD-ra-sa.
beforeReading: Write two sentences about a famous person from long ago: “He was born in 1240.” / “Most historians think he was born around 1240.” Ask which one a careful historian would write and why. Collect the words that make the difference.
duringReading: Listen for gist: What makes his works popular, and where did he study?
Color every source or certainty phrase (According to historical accounts, According to the widely accepted view, is considered, Some sources note).
Box the style sentence and the result word “Thus”.
Draw two boxes, madrasa and tekke, and put each education detail in the right box with its certainty level.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge without removing any source phrase.

Language Focus: Sort reported and direct claims (Activity 1), choose the rewrite that keeps the certainty (Activity 2), complete neither … nor / both / not limited to (Activity 3), then summarise his education cautiously (Activity 4).
Transfer: Write a short, hedged profile of a historical or family figure whose details are not fully certain.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Two sentences about a person from long ago: Which would a careful historian write?; 4–11 Listen for gist, then read and color every source or certainty phrase; 11–18 Certainty audit in groups of four: Grade the biographical sentences stated / widely accepted / attributed / some sources, then one group argues a borderline case with the class (is “He is considered the founder” certain?); 18–21 Quick Challenge; 21–31 Language Focus: Activities 1–2 in pairs with the whole-class question “why would a writer be careful here?”, Activity 3 individually, then pairs explain why “either … or” would change the meaning; 31–38 Use: Activity 4 as a 5–7 sentence summary, partners underline every hedge and check that none has been deleted; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Which biographical details are presented as certain, and which are qualified? What would be lost if we deleted the qualifiers?
Is “He is considered the founder of Turkish Sufi literature” a fact or a judgement? Who might consider him so?
How can a style be “neither too simple nor too complex” and still have literary value?
What two roles did tekkes have, according to the last paragraph?
interactiveTips: Use the Reported Facts hotspot during the certainty audit and the Madrasa and Tekke hotspot for the madrasa/tekke boxes.
Point out that the paragraph uses “According to …” twice: Once for historical accounts and once for the widely accepted view.
Reject rewrites that silently remove “some sources”, “widely accepted” or the date ranges.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a four-step certainty ladder with one example sentence on each step and the frames “According to ____, …”, “Some sources note that ____.” and “His education was not limited to ____; he also ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write an 8–10 sentence biography of a real writer or scientist using four different stance devices (according to, is considered, some sources note, the widely accepted view) and label the certainty of each sentence.

formativeAssessment: Grades claims by certainty and names the signal words.
Uses neither … nor and not limited to accurately.
Keeps approximate dates and attributions in the summary.
expectedResponses: His style is balanced, so his works have literary value and are easy to understand; according to the widely accepted view he was born in 1240–41, some sources note a good madrasa education, and his education was not limited to madrasas: He also studied divine love and morals at the tekke under a sheikh.
content.transferTask: Rewrite an overconfident claim about a historical person so that its source and certainty are explicit.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners treat the hedges as information rather than decoration, and could they justify each certainty grade with a word from the text?

classroomManagement.instructions: In groups of four, grade the biographical sentences: stated, widely accepted, attributed or some sources. Then one group argues a borderline case with the class.
checkQuestions: How many grades? (four)
What does one group argue? (a borderline case)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that 1240–41 stays approximate. During the borderline argument, ask for the signal word. In Activity 3, listen for neither … nor and not limited to. In the summary, check that every attribution is kept.

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “According to …” and one with “Some sources note that …” about a person from history, and one “neither … nor …” sentence about a book you know.

rubricLevels.secure: Grades claims by certainty and names the signal words.
Keeps the source stance in a retelling.
Uses neither … nor and not limited to accurately.
Writes a cautious summary with dates and attributions kept.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the retelling without them and ask what is missing.

interculturalFocus.notice: Yunus's style is 'neither too simple nor too complex', and the chapter separates generally accepted views from source-qualified claims about his education.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Which English poets are known for a plain but deep style (Robert Frost, William Blake)? How do English and Turkish literary critics describe such a style ('deceptively simple', 'sehl-i mümteni')?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners compare styles and keep 'is considered' for judgments, as the chapter does.

objectives: Explain the role of tekkes in the fine arts, especially poetry, and Yunus’s training under his sheikh Taptuk Emre.
Reconstruct the chain Babai uprisings → defeat at Kösedağ → Mongol invasion → hardships and distinguish time order from cause.
Discover how coincided with / was followed by (time), facilitated / as a result of (cause) and If we …, we can … (condition) organize a historical explanation.
Evaluate why the writer asks readers to study the historical atmosphere, and notice that the last paragraph (Ala al-Din Kayqubad I, 1220–1237) goes back to an earlier, stronger period.
content.pedagogy: Give the class a “relationship detective” task: Every arrow between two events must be labelled time, cause or condition, and learners may use a label only if a word in the text justifies it. This keeps chronology from turning into causation. The grammar is discovered through the labelling: Learners see that “was followed by” gives only order, that “facilitated” claims a causal link, and that “made it easier” is weaker than “caused”. Finish by asking why the chapter ends with Ala al-Din Kayqubad I’s glorious period right after a list of disasters.
priorKnowledge: Past passive (was weakened), cause and result (because of, so), first conditional.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “Facilitated” means “made easier”; the defeat at Kösedağ is not presented as the only reason for the invasion.
The Ala al-Din Kayqubad I paragraph goes back in time (1220–1237) and prepares the next chapter; it does not happen after the invasion.
The chapter does not say tekkes solved the crisis.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: time (coincided with, was immediately followed by) · cause and result (facilitated = made easier · as a result of ↔ caused / led to) · condition for interpretation (If we take a closer look …, we can better understand …).
Notice (Activity 1): learners sort five chapter sentences into time / cause and result / condition. Ask: “Does ‘This was immediately followed by the defeat at Kösedağ’ say that the uprisings caused the defeat? Which sentence does claim a cause?”
Build (Activity 2): Rewrite the chain (The defeat at Kösedağ made it easier for the Mongols to invade Anatolia · These assaults caused / led to … · The defeat at Kösedağ came immediately after this) and discuss whether “caused” is stronger than “facilitated”.
Likely errors: *facilitated the Mongols to invade · *as a result these assaults · *was followed from · *If we will take a closer look.
Use (Activity 3): 6–8 sentences explaining why the chapter asks readers to examine the historical atmosphere before interpreting Yunus, then one “If we take a closer look at …, we can better understand …” sentence about the learners’ own town or school.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Chain sentences with a pause at each link: “the anaTOlian SELjuks were SEVerely WEAKened | by the Babai UPrisings”, “this was imMEdiately FOLlowed | by the deFEAT at Kösedağ”.
The condition in two units, rising then falling: “if we take a CLOSer LOOK at this historical ATmosphere↗ | we can BETter underSTAND anaTOlia↘”.
-ed endings: weakened /d/, followed /d/, faced /t/, trained /d/, facilitated /ɪd/, coincided /ɪd/, expanded /ɪd/, established /t/.
Word focus: co-in-CID-ed, fa-CIL-i-tat-ed, in-VA-sion, AT-mos-phere, un-for-GET-ta-ble, MED-i-ter-RA-ne-an.
beforeReading: Write two events on the board: “A storm damaged the bridge.” / “The next day, the market was empty.” Ask: “Did the storm cause the empty market, or did one just come after the other? What would you need to know?” This prepares the difference between time order and cause.
duringReading: First paragraph: List what tekkes did and underline who trained Yunus.
Second paragraph: Draw the event chain in four boxes and leave the arrows unlabelled for now.
Underline the if-sentence and ask: What does the writer want the reader to do?
Last paragraph: Circle 1220–1237 and decide whether this comes before or after the invasion.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge using the event chain.
Language Focus: label time, cause and condition (Activity 1), rewrite the chain with other structures (Activity 2), then explain why context comes before interpretation (Activity 3).
Transfer: Explain one change in your town or school with a clear time phrase, a cause phrase and a hedge where you are not sure.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Storm and empty market: Cause or only sequence?; 4–11 Listen, then read and list the functions of tekkes and the four events of the crisis; 11–19 Relationship detectives in pairs: Draw Babai uprisings → Kösedağ → Mongol invasion → hardships and label each arrow time / cause / condition with the word that proves it, then a short whole-class dispute about the weakest arrow; 19–22 Quick Challenge; 22–30 Language Focus: Activity 1 checks the detectives’ labels, Activity 2 in pairs with the question “Is caused stronger than facilitated?”; 30–38 Use: Activity 3 in 6–8 sentences plus one “If we take a closer look at …, we can better understand …” sentence about their town, two volunteers read and the class says whether each link is time or cause; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Which arrows in the chain show cause and which only time order? How do you know?
Why does the writer choose “facilitated” rather than “caused”?
Why does the chapter say that studying the historical atmosphere helps us understand Anatolia and Yunus? What can context explain, and what can it not explain?
Why might the writer mention Ala al-Din Kayqubad I’s “most powerful and glorious period” right after the hardships?
interactiveTips: Use the Schools of Poets hotspot for the first paragraph and the A Chain of Disasters hotspot for the event chain.
Replay “This was immediately followed by the defeat at Kösedağ” and ask whether it states a cause.
Keep Yunus’s training under Taptuk Emre separate from the political crisis.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the four event boxes and three arrow labels (TIME / CAUSE / CONDITION) to place, plus the frames “____ was followed by ____.” and “____ made it easier for ____ to ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write an 8–10 sentence explanation that separates sequence from cause for the whole chain and ends with one hedged interpretation (This may help us understand …).

formativeAssessment: Labels time and cause links accurately with evidence.
Rephrases facilitated / as a result of without changing their strength.
Places the Ala al-Din Kayqubad I paragraph correctly in time.
expectedResponses: The Babai uprisings severely weakened the Seljuks, the defeat at Kösedağ followed and made the Mongol invasion easier, and Anatolia faced political, economic and social hardships as a result; the writer says that a closer look at this atmosphere helps us understand the land where Yunus lived.
content.transferTask: Explain one change in your town or school, separating what happened first from what caused what.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners stop treating every “then” as a “because”, and could they explain why the writer chose “facilitated”?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, draw the chain: Babai uprisings, Kösedağ, Mongol invasion, hardships. Label each arrow time, cause or condition, and write the word that proves it. Then we discuss the weakest arrow.
checkQuestions: What are the three labels? (time, cause, condition)
What do you write on each arrow? (the word that proves it)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that “made easier” is not upgraded to “caused”. In Activity 2, ask “Is caused stronger than facilitated?”. Check that the Ala al-Din Kayqubad I paragraph is placed correctly in time.

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “was followed by” and one with “as a result of” about the same local event, and say which one claims a cause.

rubricLevels.secure: Names the tekke functions with evidence.
Separates time links from cause links.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Did this cause it, or only come before it?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Rephrases without changing the strength of the claim.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Is your verb stronger than the text’s?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains the writer’s interpretive condition.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to “a closer look … helps us understand”.

interculturalFocus.notice: Tekkes supported the fine arts, especially poetry, during the hardships after Kösedağ.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Which institutions supported art and learning during hard times in other cultures (Irish monasteries copying manuscripts in the early Middle Ages)? Which in Anatolia (tekkes, medreses)?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners separate time order from cause, as the chapter does, and avoid claiming one institution saved a culture.

objectives: Build a multi-cause explanation of the crisis: Poor governance, a growing Turkmen population, migrations caused by the Mongol invasion, nomads looking for safe lands and the sultan’s failure to manage the situation.

Distinguish the writer’s general claim (“Throughout history, societies that faced difficult circumstances have always awaited a divine figure to save them”) from the specific event of 1240, and evaluate how strong the general claim is.
Discover how “even” intensifies, how due to (+ noun) differs from because (+ clause), how to + verb expresses purpose, and how a cause can be packed into a noun phrase or unpacked into a clause.
Discuss the uprising factually, without generalising about all Turkmen or judging groups beyond the text.
content.pedagogy: Lesson 1 builds a pressure map: Groups arrange five cause cards and label every arrow with the text’s own words (due to, When … were added to this, to escape, even worsened). They also evaluate the writer’s “always” generalisation and rewrite it with a hedge. Lesson 2 opens the language: Learners discover that “even” tells the reader the chaos already existed, and that the same cause can be a noun phrase (his failure to manage) or a clause (because he failed to manage). Passive and active versions are compared for what they put first.
priorKnowledge: The event chain and Ala al-Din Kayqubad I’s strong period from Chapter 3; because / because of; to + verb for purpose.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The uprising is not explained by one cause; the chapter lists several interacting pressures.
“At the time of his death” refers to Ala al-Din Kayqubad I from Chapter 3, not to Kaykhusraw II.
“Throughout history … have always awaited” is a sweeping generalisation by the writer; learners can evaluate it and hedge it instead of copying it as a fact.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: intensification with even (even worsened) · due to + noun vs because + clause · purpose with to + verb (to escape the Mongol invasion) · noun phrase ↔ clause (Kaykhusraw II’s failure to manage this situation ↔ Because Kaykhusraw II failed to manage this situation) · passive ↔ active focus (the lives of people in Anatolia were totally turned upside down ↔ they turned the lives … upside down).
Notice (Activity 1): “Kaykhusraw II’s failure to manage this situation even worsened the social and economic chaos.” Ask: “Was there chaos before his failure? Which word tells you?” Learners explain “even” before you confirm it.
Build (Activities 2–3): correct “because the poor governance” (→ due to the poor governance) and “for escape” (→ to escape), then unpack the noun phrase into a because-clause and turn the passive into the active. Ask: “Which version puts the people first, and which the migrations?”
Likely errors: *because the poor governance · *due to he governed poorly · *for escape / *for to escape · *Because his failure to manage, … · *they turned upside down the lives.
Use (Activity 4): a 7–9 sentence paragraph explaining why the Babai uprising emerged in a wider crisis, with at least three interacting causes, one due to, one even and one hedge (partly, one of the reasons).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress the turn after the high point: “the MOST POWerful and LARGest STATE in the MIDdle EAST. | HOWever, | DUE to the POOR GOVernance …”.
“Even” prepares the new information: “… even WORsened the SOcial and ecoNOMic CHAos”.
Names inside full sentences: Kaykhusraw (kay-khus-RAW), Baba Ishak, Baba Ilyas.
-ed endings: migrated /ɪd/, exhausted /ɪd/, awaited /ɪd/, worsened /d/, rebelled /d/.
Word focus: GOV-ern-ance, mi-GRA-tions, no-MAD-ic, un-REST, CIR-cum-stan-ces, di-VINE.
beforeReading: Ask: “A school suddenly has twice as many students, but nobody plans for it. What happens?” Pairs list two problems and decide whether the extra students or the poor planning is “the cause”. Keep the answer open: usually both.
duringReading: Listen for gist: Why were the lives of people in Anatolia turned upside down?
Mark five pressures: poor governance, population growth, migrations caused by the Mongol invasion, nomads looking for safe lands, the sultan’s failure to manage the situation.
Underline “even” and “When … were added to this” and say what each tells us about the pressures.
Box the general claim about societies throughout history and the specific event of 1240 separately.
afterReading: Lesson 1: Quick Challenge plus a bridge note naming three pressures that worked together.
Lesson 2: Language Focus on even (Activity 1), due to and to + verb (Activity 2), noun phrase ↔ clause and passive ↔ active (Activity 3), then the multi-cause paragraph (Activity 4).
Transfer: Explain a neutral school or town problem in which several pressures interact and poor management makes it worse.
content.lessonPlan: Lesson 1 (40 min): 0–5 Twice as many students and no planning: What is the cause?; 5–14 Listen for gist, then read and mark the five pressures; 14–26 Pressure map in groups of four: Five cause cards on the desk, every arrow labelled with the text’s own words (due to, When … were added to this, to escape, even worsened), one group presents and the others challenge any arrow the text does not support; 26–32 Evaluate the generalisation: Pairs decide whether “Throughout history, societies … have always awaited a divine figure” is a fact, an interpretation or an overgeneralisation, and rewrite it with a hedge (Many societies …, often); 32–37 Quick Challenge; 37–40 Bridge note: Three pressures that worked together; Lesson 2 (40 min): 0–4 Rebuild the pressure map from memory; 4–12 Language Focus Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Was there chaos before his failure?); 12–22 Activities 2–3 in pairs, then learners explain when they use due to and when because; 22–34 Use: Activity 4 as a 7–9 sentence multi-cause paragraph with at least one hedge; 34–38 Peer check: Partners circle every cause word and mark any sentence that names a single cause; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Which pressures existed before the migrations, and which were added? How does the chapter show that they interacted?
Why does the writer say the sultan’s failure “even worsened” the chaos rather than caused it?
Is “societies … have always awaited a divine figure” a fact or the writer’s interpretation? How could it be hedged?
How can we talk about the nomads’ situation (exhausted from wandering, looking for safe lands) with sensitivity?
interactiveTips: Use the Fleeing the Mongols hotspot for the migration pressure and the Revolt of 1240 hotspot for the event of 1240.
Replay the “even worsened” sentence and ask what already existed.
Describe Baba Ilyas’s movement only with the chapter’s words; do not add doctrinal detail.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give five cause cards with one pre-selected sentence each and the frames “Due to ____, ____ began to decline.”, “They migrated to Anatolia to ____.” and “____ even worsened ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write two explanations of the uprising (one single-cause, one multi-cause) and argue in 6–8 sentences which one the chapter supports better.

formativeAssessment: Names at least three interacting pressures with evidence.
Uses due to + noun, because + clause and to + verb for purpose accurately.
Evaluates the generalisation with appropriate hedging.
expectedResponses: After Ala al-Din Kayqubad I’s strong period, the Seljuk structure began to decline due to poor governance; the growing Turkmen population and the migrations caused by the Mongol invasion added pressure, nomads looking for safe lands caused unrest, the sultan’s failure even worsened the chaos, and in 1240 the Turkmen rebelled under Baba Ishak.
content.transferTask: Explain a neutral school or town problem in which several pressures interact and poor management makes an existing difficulty worse.
content.teacherReflection: Did the pressure map keep the explanation multi-causal, and did learners question the “always” generalisation instead of copying it?

classroomManagement.instructions: Lesson 1: In groups of four, put five cause cards on the desk. Label every arrow with the text’s own words. One group presents, and the others challenge any arrow the text does not support. Then, in pairs, evaluate the generalization.
checkQuestions: How many cause cards? (five)
What do the other groups do? (challenge unsupported arrows)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that at least three pressures interact. In the generalization task, listen for fact, interpretation or overgeneralization. In Lesson 2, check due to + noun, because + clause and to + verb.

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “due to” and one with “because” about the same problem, and one sentence with “even + verb”.

rubricLevels.secure: Names several interacting pressures with evidence.
Uses cause and purpose forms correctly.
Uses even for intensification and rewrites noun phrases as clauses.
Evaluates the generalization with hedging.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “This may be true of some …, but …”.

interculturalFocus.notice: The writer says societies in hard times 'have always awaited a divine figure to save them'. Many cultures have stories of an expected saviour.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Which legends of a returning or expected hero do you know from different cultures (King Arthur in Britain, 'the once and future king')? Why might people in crisis create or keep such stories?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners mark the writer's generalisation as an interpretation and hedge it. They do not compare the truth of religious beliefs.

objectives: Sequence the suppression of the rebellion, the capture of Erzurum (late 1242), the battle of Kösedağ (1243) and the destruction that followed, and explain the unexpected link marked by “However”.
Evaluate how the writer conveys the scale of destruction (strong verbs, a simile, extreme negatives) and why the most extreme description is introduced with “Sources say:”.
Discover how In the end, However, a date, Finally and Following … organize a historical narrative.
Discuss violence factually and with sensitivity, separating event, human consequence and source testimony.
content.pedagogy: Lesson 1 is about order and logic: Learners reconstruct the sequence and then face the puzzle of “However”: the Seljuks defeated the rebels, so why did this encourage the Mongols? Lesson 2 is about the language of scale and of sources: Learners notice the strong verbs, the simile and the extreme negatives, and that the strongest sentence belongs to “Sources”, not to the writer. Violent details are read once, calmly, and never acted out or illustrated.
priorKnowledge: The causes of the rebellion from Chapter 4; past simple narrative; linking words for sequence.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The Babai rebellion and the battle of Kösedağ are separate events; the “fathers” whom the Turkmen saw as divine saviors did not save them.
“However” here does not introduce an opposite fact but an unexpected consequence: The costly suppression encouraged the Mongols.
The most extreme description is attributed to sources; learners keep “Sources say” when they report it.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: narrative connectors (In the end, However, In late 1242, Finally, Following their easy victory at Kösedağ) · language of scale (wiped out, like a roller, leaving not a single stone standing, hardly anyone remained) · attribution with Sources say: “…” · -ing clause for a result (…, leaving behind blood, misery, and ruins).
Notice (Activity 1): learners put five mixed sentences in order using only the words at their start. Ask: “Why ‘However’ after the Seljuks won? What was unexpected?” and “What does ‘Finally’ tell us about the battle?”
Build (Activity 2): Match the four expressions of destruction with their meanings, then ask: “Which of these does the writer say himself, and which does he give to ‘Sources’? Why?”
Likely errors: *Following they won · Finally used for the first event · *In the end of the rebellion · dropping the attribution when reporting the most extreme claim.
Use (Activity 3): 6–8 sentences explaining why Kösedağ is more than a battlefield event in this chapter, connecting the battle, its aftermath and the people affected, and keeping “Sources say” for the most extreme claim.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Pause after each connector so it frames the next event: “in the END, | …”, “HOWever, | …”, “FInally, | in twelve forty-THREE, | …”, “FOLlowing their EAsy VICtory at Kösedağ, | …”.
Numbers and places: “in late twelve forty-two”, “eighty kilometres northeast of Sivas”.
-ed endings: suppressed /t/, clashed /t/, captured /d/, plundered /d/, slaughtered /d/, destroyed /d/.
Keep a calm, even voice for the sentences about killing and captivity; do not dramatise them.
Word focus: SAV-iors, sup-PRESSED, re-TREAT, PLUN-dered, CAP-tive, MER-ci-less-ly.
beforeReading: Give three event cards (the rebellion is suppressed / the Mongols capture Erzurum / the battle of Kösedağ) and ask pairs to predict the order and one possible link between the first two.
duringReading: First listening: Number the events.
Circle the word or phrase at the start of each sentence that moves the story on.
Mark with one color what the writer states and with another what “Sources say”.
Note the places on a simple outline: Erzurum, Kösedağ (80 km northeast of Sivas), Sivas, Kayseri, Erzincan.
afterReading: Lesson 1: Quick Challenge plus a bridge sentence explaining the “However” link.
Lesson 2: Language Focus: Order the sentences by their connectors (Activity 1), match the language of destruction (Activity 2), then the turning-point paragraph (Activity 3).
Transfer: Write a calm, neutral account of a turning point in a place you know, separating the event, its consequence and what sources say.
content.lessonPlan: Lesson 1 (40 min): 0–5 Predict the order of three event cards and one link; 5–14 Listen and number the events, then read to check; 14–22 “However” puzzle in pairs: Why did a Seljuk victory encourage the Mongols? each pair writes one evidence sentence and one interpretation sentence, clearly labelled; 22–30 Date-and-place line on the board: 1240, late 1242, 1243 and the places, each with one verb from the text; 30–35 Quick Challenge; 35–40 Bridge sentence on the However link; Lesson 2 (40 min): 0–4 Retrieve the date line orally; 4–12 Language Focus Activity 1 on screen, learners justify each position by its connector; 12–22 Activity 2, then a whole-class sort: Stated by the writer / attributed to sources, and a short discussion of why the writer attributes the strongest claim; 22–34 Use: Activity 3 as a 6–8 sentence turning-point paragraph in calm, factual language; 34–38 Peer check: Underline every connector and check that “Sources say” is kept; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why does the writer use “However” after the suppression of the rebellion?
What makes Kösedağ a turning point rather than just a battle, according to the chapter?
Why is the most extreme description introduced with “Sources say:”? How would the text change without it?
How can we describe destruction and suffering accurately without sensationalising it?
interactiveTips: Use the Trap at Kösedağ hotspot when learners explain how the battle was lost and the Cities in Ruins hotspot for the aftermath.
Replay the “Sources say” sentence and ask whose words these are.
Do not ask learners to role-play or draw attacks, killings or captivity.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the five sentences on strips with the connectors highlighted and the frame “In the end, ____. However, ____. Finally, ____. Following ____, ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write an 8–10 sentence account with five connectors, one -ing result clause and one attributed claim, then two sentences evaluating why the writer might attribute the strongest claim to sources.

formativeAssessment: Orders the events with connector evidence.
Explains the unexpected link marked by However.
Keeps event, consequence and source testimony distinct and calm.
expectedResponses: The Seljuks suppressed the rebellion with great difficulty, and this gave the Mongols the courage to attack; they captured Erzurum in late 1242, wiped out the Seljuk forces at Kösedağ in 1243 with a false retreat and then destroyed and plundered Sivas, Kayseri and Erzincan; sources say that hardly anyone remained in the great cities and towns.
content.transferTask: Write a calm, neutral paragraph about a turning point in a place you know, separating the event, its consequence and what sources say.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners explain the “However” link and keep the source attribution, and did both lessons stay factual and calm?

classroomManagement.instructions: Lesson 1: In pairs, solve the However puzzle: why did a Seljuk victory encourage the Mongols? Write one evidence sentence and one interpretation sentence, and label them.
checkQuestions: How many sentences? (two)
What are the labels? (evidence, interpretation)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Keep the tone calm. Check that “sources say” stays attached to the claim about empty cities. On the date line, check 1240, late 1242 and 1243 with a verb each. In Lesson 2, ask what However shows here.

exitTicket: Write three linked sentences about a school event with In the end, However and Finally.

rubricLevels.secure: Orders the events accurately.
Explains the link marked by However.
Attributes testimony to the sources.
Describes destruction calmly and without sensationalism.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “What does the text say exactly?”.

interculturalFocus.notice: The chapter describes the capture of Erzurum (1242), the Battle of Kösedağ (1243) and the destruction after it, introducing the most extreme description with 'Sources say'.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: How do Persian, Armenian and Turkish chroniclers of the 13th century describe the Mongol invasion? Why might the same event appear differently in sources from different peoples?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners describe the destruction calmly and with source language. They do not transfer blame to Mongolia or any people today.

objectives: Trace dependency as a process: weakening → small principalities in conflict → panic → agreement → dependent state → a constantly rising tax → Karatay’s relief efforts → direct attachment to the Ilkhanate in 1308.
Interpret “almost as if they were Mongols’ civil officials” as an unreal comparison and explain what it reveals.
Discover how in time, while, Nevertheless and Finally mark stages and limits, and how “led to” with noun phrases can be unpacked into clauses.
Evaluate the statesmen’s efforts fairly: The relief is acknowledged but judged “not enough”.
content.pedagogy: Lesson 1 builds a “staircase of dependency” in pairs, each step with a time or stage phrase from the text, and ends with a judgement circle: What could the statesmen do, and what could they not? Lesson 2 focuses on how the writer judges without exaggerating: Learners discover that “almost as if … were” marks an unreal comparison, that “Nevertheless” accepts an effort but says it failed, and that academic noun phrases (the weakening of …, the rapid emergence of …) can be turned into clauses.
priorKnowledge: The aftermath of Kösedağ from Chapter 5; comparatives (poorer); past continuous.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “Almost as if they were Mongols’ civil officials” does not mean the sultans literally became Mongol officials.
The agreement did not end the pressure; dependency deepened “in time”, and 1308 is the last stage, not the beginning.
“Nevertheless, these efforts were not enough” does not mean the statesmen did nothing.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: unreal comparison (almost as if they were …) · stages and limits (in time, while … were also …, Nevertheless, Finally) · led to + noun phrase ↔ clause (The weakening of the Seljuk Sultanate of Konya led to the rapid emergence of small principalities ↔ As the Seljuk Sultanate of Konya weakened, small principalities emerged rapidly) · make + object + comparative (made both the state and the people poorer).
Notice (Activity 1): “The Seljuk sultans began to act almost as if they were Mongols’ civil officials.” Ask: “Were they really officials? Which words tell you it is a comparison, not a fact?” Learners notice “as if” + past form and “almost” before you confirm it.
Build (Activities 2–3): Complete the stage words (in time / while / Nevertheless / Finally) and explain why Therefore and At first do not fit, then unpack the noun phrases into clauses (… small principalities emerged rapidly · Because this tax increased constantly, both the state and the people became poorer).
Likely errors: *as if they are · *Nevertheless of these efforts · *during trying to manage · *made the people more poor · *led to emerge.
Use (Activity 4): 7–9 sentences describing the stages by which the agreement became dependency and then direct attachment, with in time, Nevertheless and one as-if comparison.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Keep the comparison as one unit with “as if” unstressed: “began to ACT | ALmost as if they were MONgols’ CIVil ofFIcials”.
Nevertheless with a pause and a fall: “neverTHEless, | these EFforts were NOT eNOUGH↘”.
The while-sentence in two balanced halves: “on the ONE hand TRYing to MANage the MONgols, | were ALso MAKing EFforts …”.
Dates: “in thirteen oh-eight”.
Word focus: prin-ci-PAL-i-ties, e-MER-gence, de-PEN-dent, re-LIEF, of-FI-cials, IL-khan-ate.
beforeReading: Draw a staircase going down on the board. Write the first step (“The Seljuk Sultanate weakens”) and leave the last step empty. Pairs predict what the last step might be and what could happen in between.
duringReading: Listen for gist: What was the final stage?
Build the staircase: Underline every time or stage phrase (In the end, in time, began to, every year, constantly, Finally, in 1308).
Box the as-if sentence.
Mark Jalal al-Din Karatay’s two actions and the sentence that judges them.
afterReading: Lesson 1: Quick Challenge plus a bridge note naming the first and last steps of the staircase.
Lesson 2: Language Focus: The unreal comparison (Activity 1), stage and limit words (Activity 2), noun phrase ↔ clause (Activity 3), then the process paragraph (Activity 4).
Transfer: Describe how a club, team or organization gradually loses its independence, including one effort that helped but was not enough.
content.lessonPlan: Lesson 1 (40 min): 0–5 Predict the missing last step of the staircase; 5–13 Listen for gist, then read; 13–24 Staircase in pairs: Six to eight steps from the weakening of the sultanate to 1308, each with a time or stage phrase copied from the text, then pairs compare with another pair and fix one step; 24–31 Judgement circle in groups of four: What could statesmen like Jalal al-Din Karatay do, and why were their efforts “not enough”? each group gives one evidence sentence and one interpretation; 31–36 Quick Challenge; 36–40 Bridge note: First and last step; Lesson 2 (40 min): 0–4 Rebuild the staircase orally; 4–11 Language Focus Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Were they really officials?); 11–21 Activities 2–3 in pairs, then learners explain why Therefore would change the meaning of the Nevertheless sentence; 21–33 Use: Activity 4 as a 7–9 sentence process paragraph; 33–38 Pair check: Every stage has a time phrase and no sentence says the efforts solved the problem; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What does the as-if comparison tell us about the sultans’ real position?
Which words show that dependency grew gradually rather than suddenly?
How does the writer acknowledge the statesmen’s efforts and still judge them insufficient?
Why might the writer mention that the Ottoman state was still a small principality at that time?
interactiveTips: Use the Sultans as Officials hotspot for the as-if comparison and the Ilkhanate Empire hotspot for the final stage.
Replay the Karatay sentence and the Nevertheless sentence together and ask what the second one judges.
Keep the Ottoman reference to the chapter’s one sentence; do not expand it into later history.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a six-step staircase with the stage words already placed and the frames “In time, ____ became ____.”, “They acted almost as if they were ____.” and “Nevertheless, ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write an 8–10 sentence systems paragraph explaining how weakening, taxation and political dependency reinforced one another, with one unreal comparison and two noun phrases unpacked into clauses.

formativeAssessment: Sequences the stages of dependency with evidence.
Explains “as if” as an unreal comparison.
Uses Nevertheless and noun phrase ↔ clause rewrites accurately.
expectedResponses: The weakening of the sultanate led to the rapid emergence of small principalities and an atmosphere of panic; after an agreement the Seljuks in time became a dependent state, the sultans acted almost as if they were Mongol civil officials, a constantly rising tax made the state and the people poorer, Karatay’s relief efforts were not enough, and in 1308 Anatolia was directly attached to the Ilkhanate Empire.
content.transferTask: Describe how an organization gradually loses its independence, including one effort that helped but was not enough.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see dependency as a process and judge the statesmen’s efforts fairly, neither ignoring nor overstating them?

classroomManagement.instructions: Lesson 1: In pairs, build a staircase of six to eight steps from the weakening of the sultanate to 1308. Copy a time or stage phrase onto each step. Then compare with another pair and fix one step.
checkQuestions: How many steps? (six to eight)
What do you do with another pair? (compare and fix one step)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that 1308 is the last step. In the judgement circle, listen for one evidence sentence and one interpretation. In Lesson 2, ask what as if shows. Check Nevertheless and noun ↔ clause rewrites.

exitTicket: Write one “almost as if … were …” sentence about school life and one sentence with “Nevertheless”.

rubricLevels.secure: Sequences the stages of dependence.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the first and last steps.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains as if as an unreal comparison.
Uses stage language and Nevertheless correctly.
Gives a balanced judgement of Karatay’s efforts.

interculturalFocus.notice: The Seljuk sultans became 'almost as if they were Mongols' civil officials', and Karatay tried to bring relief.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Which English and Turkish terms describe a state that depends on another ('vassal', 'puppet state'; 'tâbi devlet', 'kukla devlet')? Which terms are neutral and which are loaded?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners choose neutral terms for academic writing and explain why loaded terms can be unfair.

content.chapter: Chapter 7: Yunus Appears as a Wise Dervish
objectives: Connect the chaos in Anatolia with Yunus’s appearance as a wise dervish and his response through poetry.

Name the sources on which his understanding of Sufism is based (the Qur’an and the Sunnah, as well as the thoughts and experiences of earlier Muslim Sufis) and explain the chapter’s definition of Sunnah.

Discover how short phrases pack circumstance, time, perspective and means into one sentence (under Mongol pressure, During the same period, through the lens of his Sufi identity, using poetry as his medium).
Evaluate what the chapter says poetry did (respond to people’s efforts to make sense of life) and what it does not claim (that poetry ended the political crisis).
content.pedagogy: Build a context → perspective → medium → sources chain on the board and let pairs fill each link with a phrase from the text. Then compress and expand: Learners discover that the writer packs a whole clause into a short phrase (under Mongol pressure = because the Mongols pressured them) and practise unpacking and repacking. Close with an evaluation: What does the text say poetry did, and what does it not say?
priorKnowledge: The historical crisis from Chapters 4–6; relative clauses with who/which; -ing participles.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The chapter does not say Yunus ended the crisis; it says he tried to respond to people’s efforts to make sense of life in hard days.
“Through the lens of” is a metaphor for a point of view, not a physical lens.
The shaykhs came “under Mongol pressure”; they were not part of the Mongol invasion.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: compact phrases for circumstance, time, perspective and means (under Mongol pressure · During the same period · through the lens of his Sufi identity · using poetry as his medium) · participle phrase ↔ and-clause · relative who instead of a repeated noun · a which-clause that defines (the Sunnah, which is the collective term for the sayings, actions, and approvals of the Prophet (pbuh)).
Notice (Activity 1): learners match five phrases with their meanings. Ask: “What is a lens for? So what does ‘through the lens of his Sufi identity’ mean?”
Build (Activity 2): unpack and join (… and he used poetry as his medium · These shaykhs raised dervishes on their teachings, who were dominant among nomads · … because the Mongols pressured them) and discuss which version is more compact and which is clearer.
Likely errors: *using poetry like his medium · *dervishes, which were dominant · *during Yunus lived (during + clause) · *under the Mongols pressure.
Use (Activity 3): 5–7 sentences explaining how the chapter moves from crisis to Yunus’s response, with at least one compact phrase for circumstance and one for means.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Chunk the long sentence into meaning units with short pauses: “he TRIED to reSPOND | to PEOple’s EFforts | to make SENSE of LIFE in HARD DAYS | through the LENS of his SUfi iDENtity, | USing POetry as his MEdium”.
Place names in a list, rising on each and falling on the last: Tur-kes-TAN↗, trans-ox-i-A-na↗, Kho-ra-SAN↗, Khwa-REZM↗ and i-RAN↘.
Word focus: DER-vish, DOM-i-nant, ME-di-um, col-LEC-tive, ap-PROV-als, i-DEN-ti-ty.
beforeReading: Ask: “In hard times, people need food and safety. What else do they need?” Collect answers (hope, meaning, community, songs, stories) and ask which of these a poet could offer and which a poet could not.
duringReading: Listen for gist: What did Yunus do “in such an environment”?
Mark the context: Total chaos, shaykhs under Mongol pressure, dervishes among nomads, popular Sufism.
Underline Yunus’s response and circle the means (poetry).
Box the sources of his understanding and the definition of Sunnah.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the chain visible.
Language Focus: Match the compact phrases (Activity 1), unpack and join sentences (Activity 2), then write the crisis-to-response paragraph (Activity 3).
Transfer: Describe how someone in your community responded to a hard time through art, sport or words, and what they could not change.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook: What else do people need in hard times? which of these can a poet offer?; 5–12 Listen for gist, then read and underline Yunus’s response; 12–19 Chain on the board: context / perspective / medium / sources, pairs fill one link each with a quoted phrase and defend it; 19–22 Quick Challenge; 22–30 Language Focus: Activity 1 in pairs with the lens question, Activity 2 in pairs, then a quick “pack it / unpack it” round (you say a clause, learners give the compact phrase); 30–38 Use: Activity 3 in 5–7 sentences plus one limitation sentence (The chapter does not claim that …); 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: How does the chapter connect the chaos in Anatolia with Yunus’s appearance as a wise dervish?
What does “through the lens of his Sufi identity” suggest about how he saw people’s problems?
What does the chapter say poetry did, and what would be an unsupported claim about it?
On which sources is his understanding of Sufism based, according to the chapter?
interactiveTips: Use the Popular Sufism hotspot for the dervishes among nomads and the Poetry as a Medium hotspot for Yunus’s response.
Replay the long sentence about his response and let learners mark the pauses.
Keep the definition of Sunnah exactly as the chapter gives it.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give four headings (Context / Perspective / Medium / Sources) with one sentence for each and the frames “____ came to Anatolia under ____.” and “He responded through ____, using ____ as his medium.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write an 8–10 sentence analysis of how the chapter is built (context, response, sources) with three compact phrases and one sentence that limits the claim about poetry.

formativeAssessment: Links context and response with evidence.
Explains the compact phrases and can unpack them into clauses.
Names the sources of his understanding accurately and does not overstate the power of poetry.
expectedResponses: In the chaos of Anatolia, shaykhs came under Mongol pressure and their dervishes spread a popular Sufism among nomads; Yunus emerged as a wise dervish and tried to respond to people’s efforts to make sense of life through the lens of his Sufi identity, using poetry as his medium; his understanding is based on the Qur’an and the Sunnah as well as on earlier Muslim Sufis.
content.transferTask: Describe someone who responded to a hard time in your community through art, sport or words, and say what they could not change.
content.teacherReflection: Could learners unpack the compact phrases, and did they keep the claim about poetry within the chapter’s wording?

classroomManagement.instructions: Look at the chain on the board: context, perspective, medium, sources. In pairs, fill one link with a quoted phrase and defend it to the class.
checkQuestions: How many links? (four)
How many links does each pair fill? (one)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that the medium is poetry and the lens is his Sufi identity. During pack it and unpack it, give one clause at a time. In the Use task, check the limitation sentence.

exitTicket: Rewrite “under Mongol pressure” as a because-clause, and write one sentence about yourself with “using … as my …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Links the context and Yunus’s response with evidence.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “What problem was he responding to?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains compact phrases and unpacks them into clauses.
Names the sources of his thought accurately.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the Qur’an, the Sunnah and earlier Sufis.

rubricLevels.secure: Writes a qualified claim about the power of poetry.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “The chapter does not claim that …”.

interculturalFocus.notice: Yunus responded to the crisis 'through the lens of his Sufi identity', through poetry.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Which artists or poets responded to crisis in other countries and periods (war poets in Britain during the First World War, Mehmet Âkif during the War of Independence)? What could their words change, and what could they not?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners keep the chapter's limit: poetry can help people reflect but does not remove the material problem.

objectives: Define tawhid exactly as the chapter does (the absolute Oneness of Allah).

Separate the definition, the views attributed to Yunus Emre, the theory of the Unity of Existence and Yunus’s own poem, and explain why the writer uses “According to …” for some ideas and “Yunus says:” for others.
Discover how From this perspective, for this reason and Nonetheless build an argument step by step.
Discuss theological ideas respectfully and within the chapter’s wording, assessing understanding and language, not personal belief.
content.pedagogy: Voices and steps organize both lessons. In Lesson 1 learners color-code the chapter (definition / according to Yunus / according to the theory / poem / writer’s conclusion) and read the poem in meaning groups. In Lesson 2 they discover that “According to X” tells us whose idea it is without agreeing or disagreeing, and that each linking expression makes a different logical move (following from a viewpoint, cause → result, true in spite of). Learners are not asked to debate or extend the theology beyond the text.
priorKnowledge: Source stance from Chapter 2; which-clauses; therefore.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “According to …” does not mean the writer disagrees, nor that every scholar accepts the idea.
Vahdet-i vücut is presented as a theory Yunus held; learners should not generalise it to all Muslims or all Sufis.
“Nonetheless” does not deny that multiple existence emerged; it adds that this multiplicity is still nothing but manifestations of the names of Allah.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: attribution (According to Yunus Emre, … · According to the theory of the Unity of Existence, …) vs quotation (Yunus says: “…”) · definition with which means · argument links (therefore, From this perspective, for this reason, As a result of, Nonetheless) · nothing but for exclusive focus.
Notice (Activity 1): learners compare the two “According to …” openings and choose why the writer uses them. Ask: “Does the writer agree, disagree or simply tell us whose idea it is? How does the chapter introduce Yunus’s own words?”
Build (Activity 2): choose From this perspective / for this reason / Nonetheless in three chapter sentences and name the logical move each makes (follows from a viewpoint / cause → result / true in spite of what was just said).
Likely errors: *According to Yunus Emre’s opinion, he thinks … (double attribution) · Nonetheless used like Therefore · *which mean · *For this reason of ….
Use (Activity 3): 6–8 sentences explaining the chapter’s connection between tawhid, true reality and creation, with every claim attributed (According to …, The chapter presents …).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Pause after every attribution so the owner of the idea is clear: “acCORDing to YUnus EMre, | the creATor, alLAH | is the SOURCE of ALL THINGS”.
The definition clause on a slightly lower pitch: “the beLIEF in TAWhid, | which MEANS the ABsolute ONEness of alLAH”.
Read the poem line by line with a pause at the semicolon, calmly and without preaching intonation: “the enTIRE UNiverse is TAWhid; | ADam is the ONE who KNOWS TAWhid”.
Word focus: TAW-hid, AB-so-lute, AT-tri-butes, man-i-fes-TA-tions, dis-IN-te-grat-ed, none-the-LESS; vahdet-i vücut is read as in Turkish.
beforeReading: Write two sentences: “The Earth goes round the Sun.” / “According to my grandfather, the best tea comes from Rize.” Ask what “According to” does and whether it shows agreement or disagreement.
duringReading: Listen for gist: What is tawhid, according to the chapter?
Box the definition and underline both “According to …” openings.
Circle the linking expressions (therefore, From this perspective, for this reason, As a result of, Nonetheless).
Treat the poem as a separate voice introduced by “Yunus says:”.
afterReading: Lesson 1: Quick Challenge plus a bridge note with one definition and one attributed statement.
Lesson 2: Language Focus on attribution (Activity 1) and argument links (Activity 2), then the attributed explanation (Activity 3).
Transfer: Explain an idea from science or another subject step by step, attributing each view to its source.
content.lessonPlan: Lesson 1 (40 min): 0–5 Earth and Sun / grandfather’s tea: What does “According to” do?; 5–14 Listen and read; 14–25 Color-coding in pairs: definition / according to Yunus / according to the theory / poem / writer’s conclusion, each color with one quoted sentence; 25–32 Poem in meaning groups: Learners say in plain words what each half-line claims, without extending it; 32–37 Quick Challenge; 37–40 Bridge note; Lesson 2 (40 min): 0–4 Retrieve the color-coding; 4–11 Language Focus Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (agree, disagree or tell us whose idea?); 11–20 Activity 2 in pairs, each pair names the logical move of one link and teaches it to the class; 20–32 Use: Activity 3 in 6–8 sentences with every claim attributed; 32–37 Source-boundary check: Partners mark any sentence that sounds more certain or more general than the chapter; 37–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What does the chapter define directly, and what does it attribute to Yunus or to a theory?
Why does the writer use “Yunus says:” for the poem rather than “According to Yunus”?
What logical move does each of these make: From this perspective, for this reason, Nonetheless?
What wording would make an attributed claim sound falsely universal?
interactiveTips: Use the Source of All Things hotspot for the attributed claim and the Unity of Existence hotspot for the theory.
Replay both “According to …” sentences before learners paraphrase.
Do not turn the lesson into a theological debate; assess understanding and attribution, not belief.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a color key and the frames “Tawhid means ____.”, “According to Yunus Emre, ____.” and “For this reason, ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write an 8–10 sentence explanation with three different attribution frames and three argument links, and label the logical move of each link in the margin.

formativeAssessment: Defines tawhid from the text.
Attributes every view correctly and distinguishes attribution from quotation.
Explains the logical move of each link.
expectedResponses: The chapter defines tawhid as the absolute Oneness of Allah; according to Yunus, Allah is the source of all things and the true and only reality, and according to the theory of the Unity of Existence, Allah desired to be known and for this reason created the worlds through His attributes; the multiple existence that emerged is nonetheless nothing but manifestations of the names of Allah.
content.transferTask: Explain a scientific or school idea step by step, attributing each view to its source and marking each logical move.
content.teacherReflection: Did every paraphrase keep its owner, and could learners explain the difference between from this perspective, for this reason and nonetheless?

classroomManagement.instructions: Lesson 1: In pairs, color-code the chapter: definition, according to Yunus, according to the theory, poem and writer’s conclusion. Quote one sentence for each. Then say in plain words what each half-line of the poem claims.
checkQuestions: How many colors? (five)
Do you extend the poem’s meaning? (no)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that tawhid is defined from the text. Make sure every view has its owner. Stop any expansion beyond the text. In Lesson 2, ask “agree, disagree, or tell us whose idea?”.

exitTicket: Write one “…, which means …” sentence and one “According to …, …” sentence about an idea from another subject.

rubricLevels.secure: Defines tawhid from the text.
Separates attribution from quotation.
Explains the logical move of each link.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “What does this word do here?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Stays inside the source.

interculturalFocus.notice: The chapter defines tawhid and attributes the theory of the Unity of Existence (vahdet-i vücûd) to a school of thought.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: How do English academic texts render terms like 'vahdet-i vücûd' (the Unity of Being / of Existence)? Why do translators sometimes give two English versions?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners practise attributing views to their sources across languages, without simplifying a complex idea into a slogan.

objectives: Explain the chapter’s chain from “everything which is created is a reflection” to the ultimate purpose of humanity, Allah’s commands and love.
Show how the prayer verse (Allah’s command, the five daily prayers) and the love paragraphs stand together, without one replacing the other.

Discover how the writer states goals (The ultimate purpose of … is to …), draws conclusions (In this sense, Therefore, From this perspective) and gives a reason with formal For, and how fixed expressions (stand out, lie at the core of, extend to) show that love is central.
Interpret the two-way relationship “those who love the Creator love the created, and those who love the created also love the Creator”.
content.pedagogy: Give each pair the chapter’s key sentences on strips and ask them to label each one goal, conclusion or reason. Learners discover that the labels depend on small words (In this sense, Therefore, For) and argue about which conclusion follows from what. A short second task treats the fixed expressions as “centrality language”: learners find the ways the writer shows that love is central. Keep the prayer verse and the love paragraphs visibly side by side on the board.
priorKnowledge: Attribution and argument links from Chapter 8; purpose with to + verb.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The chapter does not say love replaces the commands or prayer; the verse and the love paragraphs stand side by side.
Sentence-initial “For” means “because” here, not “for example”.
The poem’s “should” expresses what is expected of a Muslim; the verse is read and explained, not rewritten.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: goal (The ultimate purpose of humanity is to reach unity with Allah · The purpose of love is to reach Allah …) · conclusion (In this sense, Therefore, From this perspective) · reason with formal For (For, according to him, where love is absent, negative emotions … arise) · fixed expressions of centrality (stands out, lies at the core of, extends to).
Notice (Activity 1): learners sort six chapter sentences into goal / conclusion / reason. Ask: “What does ‘For’ mean at the start of the last sentence? Which claim is it explaining?”
Build (Activity 2): Complete “stands out”, “lies at the core of” and “extends to”, then explain in their own words how each expression makes love look central.
Likely errors: *The purpose of love is reach · *stands up in his works · *lies in the core of · *extends until · sentence-initial For read as “for example”.
Use (Activity 3): 6–8 sentences explaining how the chapter moves from “everything is a reflection” to love, harmony and religious practice, with one goal sentence, one conclusion link and one For-reason.
content.pronunciationFocus:
The mirror sentence needs a clear rhythm, with the stress on “ALso” in the second half: “those who love the CreATor | love the creATed, | and those who love the creATed | ALso love the CreATor”.
Formal For with a pause: “FOR, | acCORDing to HIM, | where LOVE is ABsent, | …”.
Fixed expressions as single chunks: STANDS OUT, lies at the CORE of, exTENDS to.
Word focus: UL-ti-mate, HAR-mo-ny, in-ter-re-LAT-ed, re-QUIRE-ments, ES-sence, foun-DA-tion.
beforeReading: Ask: “Can two things be deeply connected without one replacing the other, for example rules and friendship in a team?” Pairs give one example and keep it for the end of the lesson.
duringReading: Listen for gist: What is the ultimate purpose of humanity, according to the chapter?
Mark the goal sentences, the conclusion words and the sentence that starts with “For”.
Keep the prayer verse and the love paragraphs in two boxes and draw the line that connects them (Allah’s commands “for achieving this unity”).
Underline the mirror sentence about loving the Creator and the created.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge.
Language Focus: Sort goal / conclusion / reason (Activity 1), complete the centrality expressions (Activity 2), then write the connected explanation (Activity 3).
Transfer: Explain how two values in school or family life (for example rules and friendship) are connected without one replacing the other.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Team rules and friendship: Connected without replacing each other?; 4–11 Listen for gist, then read with the prayer verse and the love paragraphs in two boxes; 11–19 Argument strips in pairs: The chapter’s key sentences on strips, pairs label each one goal / conclusion / reason and name the word that decided it, then one disputed strip is discussed with the class; 19–22 Quick Challenge; 22–30 Language Focus: Activity 1 confirms the strip labels, Activity 2 in pairs, then learners find two more centrality phrases in the chapter (at the foundation of, at the essence of); 30–38 Use: Activity 3 in 6–8 sentences, one volunteer reads and the class names every link; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: How does the chapter link “everything which is created is a reflection” with the ultimate purpose of humanity?
How do the prayer verse and the love paragraphs relate? What would be an unsupported claim about them?
What could the mirror sentence about the Creator and the created mean for how people treat each other?
What reason does the writer give, with “For”, for saying that love and unity are interrelated?
interactiveTips: Use the Five Daily Prayers hotspot for the verse and the Love Brings Unity hotspot for the final paragraphs.
Read the verse phrase by phrase and never gap or rewrite it.
Replay the last sentence and ask what “For” means there.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the three labels with one example each and the frames “The ultimate purpose of ____ is to ____.”, “Therefore, ____.” and “Love lies at the core of ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write an 8–10 sentence analysis of the chapter’s argument, labelling each step (goal, conclusion, reason) and using two centrality expressions.

formativeAssessment: Labels argument moves with evidence from the linking words.
Keeps commands and love side by side without substitution.
Uses the fixed expressions accurately.
expectedResponses: Everything created is a reflection and the ultimate purpose of humanity is to reach unity with Allah; Yunus’s words remind us of Allah’s commands, such as the five daily prayers; love lies at the core of his philosophy, so those who love the Creator love the created; love and unity are interrelated because, according to him, where love is absent, anger, heartbreak and separation arise.
content.transferTask: Explain how two values in school or family life are connected without one replacing the other.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners use the linking words to follow the argument, and did they keep the commands and love connected without substitution?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, label the key sentence strips goal, conclusion or reason. Name the word that decided each label. Then we discuss one disputed strip together.
checkQuestions: What are the three labels? (goal, conclusion, reason)
What do you name for each strip? (the word that decided it)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that commands and love are kept side by side, not one replacing the other. In Activity 2, ask learners to find at the foundation of and at the essence of. In the Use task, check the connected explanation.

rubric: Commands and love side by side
exitTicket: Write one “The ultimate purpose of … is to …” sentence about your class and one sentence with “lies at the core of”.

rubricLevels.secure: Labels argument moves with evidence.

rubricLevels.criterion: Commands and love side by side
rubricLevels.secure: Keeps commands and love side by side.
Uses centrality expressions accurately.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give at the core of as a model.

rubricLevels.secure: Writes a connected explanation.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the three link words as a checklist.

interculturalFocus.notice: The chapter says everything created is a reflection and that love of the Creator includes love of the created. Yunus's line 'Yaratılanı severiz Yaratandan ötürü' is often quoted in Türkiye.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: How would you translate that line into English so that it keeps its rhythm and meaning? Compare your version with a classmate's. What is lost and what is gained?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Translation is an intercultural act. Learners accept that more than one good translation can exist.

objectives: Explain the heart as “the throne of the Lord” and the moral conclusion the writer draws from it (breaking a heart as destroying Allah’s house).
Classify the three types of intellect (the practical reason, the limited intellect, the universal intellect) with their functions and keep Yunus’s positive view of intellect.
Discover how which-clauses define, how “that is” + “the place where” clarifies, how “describe … as” works and why a subject joined with “and” takes a plural verb.
Distinguish a metaphor from a literal claim and draw a responsible ethical inference from it.
