standardisation: Before scoring, read the B2 descriptors for written and spoken production in the CEFR table of this book.

With a colleague, score the same three writing papers on your own with the B2 writing bands (Task, Organisation, Grammar, Vocabulary). Then compare and talk about any criterion where your scores differ by more than one band.
Score one speaking test together in the same way: both listen, both score, then compare.
Keep one agreed paper for each band as a sample for later scoring.

selfAssessment.prompt: Chapter 3: Could learners do this by the end of the lesson: “Explain the role of tekkes in the fine arts, especially poetry, and Yunus’s training under his sheikh Taptuk Emre”? Which stage of the lesson flow helped most, and which did not?
Chapter 5 is planned for 40 + 40 minutes. Which stage took longer than planned, and what did you move to the next lesson?
Before the pair or group work in Chapter 6, did you ask “How many steps?” How many learners could answer before they started?
In Chapter 13, how many learners were secure on “Verse interpretation”? What did you do for those who were not yet secure?

When you asked “How do English academic texts render terms like 'vahdet-i vücûd' (the Unity of Being / of Existence)?” in Chapter 8, did learners describe other cultures with facts or with stereotypes? Which words did you give them?

Which of the likely errors listed for Chapter 10 did you hear (*the love and the oneness of Allah is · *the place which Allah manifests Himself · *described … like · *not only heart but intellect)? Did you correct them during the activity or after it, and why?
Which app tools did your learners use with this book (audio, Word Notes, the exercises and their result codes)? Which one gave you the most useful information about their learning?
Read your reflection log for this book. What is one change you will make the next time you teach this book, and who will you share it with?

actionResearch.question: Do learners hedge their claims about a historical person (Chapter 2: is considered, the widely accepted view) as the chapter does?
steps: Baseline: in the Chapter 2 transfer task, count learners who use one hedge correctly.
Recycle: in Chapters 4 and 13, ask learners to rewrite one strong claim with a hedge.
Check: after the B2 End-of-Level Test, note item 22 (tend to for hedging) for the class in Score a test, and read the writing papers for hedges.
Decide: list the hedges learners use and plan one practice for the ones they avoid.

collaboration: Share your counts for tend to for hedging with another English teacher who uses this book, and agree on one activity to try in both classes.
Plan the Chapter 9 lesson with the Turkish literature teacher: learners compare two English translations of 'Yaratılanı severiz Yaratandan ötürü'.

objectives: I can explain the outer and the inner sides of a Sufi lifestyle.
I can explain why Yunus Emre matters in two different fields.
I can add a second role with “In addition to” + noun or -ing.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Decide what “whereas” does in the outer–inner sentence (it contrasts two sides that Sufis keep), add a second identity with “In addition” or “In addition to being”, then correct two forms after a preposition: “of becoming” and “without expecting”. The last activity asks you to explain Yunus’s importance in two different but connected fields.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: SÛ-fî, MYS-ti-cism, CRU-cial, GEN-er-ous-ly, LIT-er-ar-y. Read the long list of principles in paragraph 1 with a short pause at each comma, and let your voice fall only at the end.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Outer and Inner”. Which side is about the body and which is about the heart? Listen once and decide what each paragraph is about. Read paragraph 1 again and number the Sufi principles in the long list.
discussionPoints: Sufis try to do good to all individuals without prejudice and to answer evil with kindness. Which of these principles is the hardest to practise, and why?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Plain Turkish” and “Outer and Inner”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Say in five words what paragraph 1 does. Read the first sentence of paragraph 2, especially “In addition to his standing as a Sufi”. Choose the option that describes something new in paragraph 2, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Explain how the chapter presents Yunus as important in two fields, the spiritual and the literary. Link them with “In addition to …” and show how one supports the other without reducing either.

whatToNotice: The chapter has two paragraphs with two jobs: The first defines a Sufi and lists Sufi principles, the second turns to Yunus as a poet and his role in the Turkish language.

Notice “The outer part relates to the body’s acts of worship, whereas the inner side handles the morality and intentions of the heart.” “Whereas” contrasts two sides that Sufis keep together; it does not ask you to choose one.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Outer and Inner”. Which side is about the body and which is about the heart?
Listen once and decide what each paragraph is about.
Read paragraph 1 again and number the Sufi principles in the long list.
Open the picture hotspots “Plain Turkish” and “Outer and Inner” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find the definition of a Sufi and the two norms of Islam that Sufis live within.
Paragraph 1: find the principles about giving, doing good and worldly possessions.
Paragraph 2: find what Yunus was one of the first to do and what his words contributed to.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: Islamic mysticism, crucial, moral principles, generously, literary tradition.
“the act of giving generously without expecting any return”. What does “without expecting any return” add to the meaning of generously?
Write one sentence with crucial and one with literary tradition about a writer you know.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks about the purpose of the second paragraph. Read its opening words and compare them with what paragraph 1 was about.
wrongAnswerSupport: Say in five words what paragraph 1 does.
Read the first sentence of paragraph 2, especially “In addition to his standing as a Sufi”.
Choose the option that describes something new in paragraph 2, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain the outer and the inner side?
Can I name Yunus’s two fields?
Can I correct “without expect any return”?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Explain how the chapter presents Yunus as important in two fields, the spiritual and the literary. Link them with “In addition to …” and show how one supports the other without reducing either.
content.reflectionPrompt: Sufis try to do good to all individuals without prejudice and to answer evil with kindness. Which of these principles is the hardest to practise, and why?

objectives: I can separate claims the writer reports from claims the writer states directly.
I can compare Yunus’s madrasa and tekke education.
I can keep a source’s level of certainty when I rewrite a claim.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Sort six sentences into claims the writer reports or qualifies and claims stated directly, choose the rewrite that keeps “the widely accepted view” (“Most scholars accept that …”), then complete the lines with “neither … nor”, “both” and “not limited to”. The last activity asks you to summarise his education without making uncertain details sound certain.
content.pronunciationFocus: Names: ha-JI bek-TASH-i VE-li, mev-LA-na, SA-ru sal-TUK. Stress: con-TEM-po-rar-y, sol-i-DAR-i-ty, MAD-ra-sa. Give neither and nor equal stress: NEI-ther too simple NOR too complex.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Reported Facts”. Which phrases present a detail as reported? Listen once for his style, his dates and his education. Read again and mark every source phrase in one color and every direct statement in another.
discussionPoints: His works have literary value and are also easy to understand. Why might clear, simple language reach more people without losing depth?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Reported Facts” and “Madrasa and Tekke”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: List the source phrases in paragraphs 2 and 3. Match each option to its phrase, or to no phrase at all. Choose the option that sits after “Some sources note that”, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Summarise Yunus’s education in four to five sentences. Keep “Some sources note” or a similar hedge for the madrasa details, state the tekke’s role directly, and join the two with “not limited to”.

whatToNotice: Biographical details are framed with care: “According to historical accounts”, “According to the widely accepted view”, “He is considered”, “Some sources note that”.
Notice “His style is neither too simple nor too complex.” This is the writer’s own direct judgment, with no source phrase.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Reported Facts”. Which phrases present a detail as reported?
Listen once for his style, his dates and his education.
Read again and mark every source phrase in one color and every direct statement in another.
Open the picture hotspots “Reported Facts” and “Madrasa and Tekke” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find the two qualities his works have because of his style.
Paragraph 2: find his famous contemporaries and his dates, and the phrase that frames each.
Paragraphs 3–4: find what he learned at the madrasa and at the tekke, and the wider role of tekkes.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: contemporary, solidarity, civil society, madrasas, spiritual tutor.
“tekkes were not just institutions that offered Sufi training”. What else were they, according to paragraph 4?
Write one sentence with solidarity and one with contemporary.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks which claim the writer attributes to some sources. Find “Some sources note that” at the start of paragraph 3 and read to the end of that sentence.
wrongAnswerSupport: List the source phrases in paragraphs 2 and 3.
Match each option to its phrase, or to no phrase at all.
Choose the option that sits after “Some sources note that”, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I name three source phrases in the chapter?
Can I compare the madrasa and the tekke?
Can I explain why “proven beyond doubt” overclaims?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Summarise Yunus’s education in four to five sentences. Keep “Some sources note” or a similar hedge for the madrasa details, state the tekke’s role directly, and join the two with “not limited to”.
content.reflectionPrompt: His works have literary value and are also easy to understand. Why might clear, simple language reach more people without losing depth?

objectives: I can explain the tekke’s role in poetry and in Yunus’s training.
I can follow a chain of events from the Babai uprisings to hardship.
I can express time, cause and condition with different structures.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Sort sentences into time (coincided with, was followed by), cause and result (facilitated, as a result of) and condition (If we take a closer look …), then rewrite the chain with “made it easier”, “caused” or “led to”, and “came immediately after”. The last activity asks you to explain why the chapter examines the historical atmosphere before interpreting Yunus.
content.pronunciationFocus: Names: TAP-tuk EM-re, KÖ-se-dağ, a-la-ed-DIN. Stress: co-in-CID-ed, fa-CIL-i-tat-ed, in-VA-sion. Read the dates as twelve twenty to twelve thirty-seven.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “A Chain of Disasters”. How many disasters does it name? Listen once and follow the chain in paragraph 2. Read paragraph 2 again and circle “followed by”, “facilitated” and “as a result of”.
discussionPoints: Yunus lived and wrote in a time of invasion and hardship. How can knowing the hard times of a writer change the way you read the writer’s words?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Schools of Poets” and “A Chain of Disasters”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 2. Write each event on its own line and put the linking word next to it. Order the events again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Explain in five to six sentences why the chapter asks you to look at the historical atmosphere first. Use one time link, one cause link and one condition with “If we …, we can …”.

whatToNotice: The chapter moves from the tekke, to a chain of disasters, to a reason for studying history, and then back to a strong sultan.
Notice “If we take a closer look at this historical atmosphere, we can better understand Anatolia”. The writer explains why the next chapters are about history, not poetry.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “A Chain of Disasters”. How many disasters does it name?
Listen once and follow the chain in paragraph 2.
Read paragraph 2 again and circle “followed by”, “facilitated” and “as a result of”.
Open the picture hotspots “Schools of Poets” and “A Chain of Disasters” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find the field in which tekkes led and the name of Yunus’s sheikh.
Paragraph 2: find the four steps from the Babai uprisings to the hardships of society.
Paragraph 4: find the dates of Ala al-Din Kayqubad I and two things he did.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: fine arts, coincided, facilitated, invasion, navy.
“The defeat at Kösedağ facilitated the Mongols' invasion of Anatolia.” Does facilitated mean the defeat was the only cause of the invasion?
Write one sentence with coincided and one with facilitated.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will put the steps of the hard times in order. Paragraph 2 gives them in order, joined by linking words.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 2.
Write each event on its own line and put the linking word next to it.
Order the events again.
selfCheck: Can I explain what tekkes did for poetry?
Can I retell the chain in four steps?
Can I turn “as a result of these assaults” into a sentence with caused?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Explain in five to six sentences why the chapter asks you to look at the historical atmosphere first. Use one time link, one cause link and one condition with “If we …, we can …”.
content.reflectionPrompt: Yunus lived and wrote in a time of invasion and hardship. How can knowing the hard times of a writer change the way you read the writer’s words?

objectives: I can explain several causes of the crisis in Anatolia.
I can tell a general claim from the specific case it prepares.
I can use “due to” + noun and “to” + verb for purpose correctly.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Decide what “even” adds (the chaos already existed and got worse), correct “due to the poor governance” and “to escape”, then turn noun phrases into clauses: “Because Kaykhusraw II failed to manage this situation …” and “they turned the lives … upside down”. The last activity asks you to explain the uprising as part of a wider crisis.
content.pronunciationFocus: Names: gi-ya-sed-DIN key-hüs-REV, BA-ba is-HAK, BA-ba il-YAS, TÜRK-men. Stress: de-CLINE, no-MAD-ic, un-REST, re-BELLED. Put light stress on “even” in “even worsened”.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Fleeing the Mongols”. Why were the tribes exhausted? Listen once and count the causes of the chaos. Read paragraph 1 again and number each cause.
discussionPoints: The writer says societies in hard times have always waited for a saviour. Is this a fact, an interpretation, or both? What would you need to support it?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Fleeing the Mongols” and “The Revolt of 1240”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to the start of paragraph 2. Read “The Turkmen, too, were awaiting such a figure.” and the sentence about 1240. Ask what the general sentence prepares you for, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write a paragraph that explains why the Babai uprising happened in a wider crisis. Show how at least three causes worked together, and use “due to”, “because” + clause and “even”.

whatToNotice: Paragraph 1 adds pressure on pressure: Poor governance, a growing Turkmen population, migrations, unrest and a failed response.
Notice “Throughout history, societies that faced difficult circumstances have always awaited a divine figure to save them.” This is the writer’s general interpretation, not a fact about one group.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Fleeing the Mongols”. Why were the tribes exhausted?
Listen once and count the causes of the chaos.
Read paragraph 1 again and number each cause.
Open the picture hotspots “Fleeing the Mongols” and “The Revolt of 1240” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find whose poor governance started the decline and his dates.
Paragraph 1: find where the nomadic tribes came from and what they were looking for.
Paragraph 2: find when the Turkmen rebelled, under whose leadership, and who founded the movement.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: decline, nomadic, poor governance, unrest, rebelled.
“Kaykhusraw II’s failure to manage this situation even worsened the social and economic chaos.” What does even tell you about the chaos before his failure?
Write one sentence with unrest and one with poor governance.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why paragraph 2 opens with a sentence about all societies. Read the two sentences that come straight after it.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to the start of paragraph 2.
Read “The Turkmen, too, were awaiting such a figure.” and the sentence about 1240.
Ask what the general sentence prepares you for, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I name three causes of the chaos?
Can I explain what “even worsened” means?
Can I correct “for escape the Mongol invasion”?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write a paragraph that explains why the Babai uprising happened in a wider crisis. Show how at least three causes worked together, and use “due to”, “because” + clause and “even”.
content.reflectionPrompt: The writer says societies in hard times have always waited for a saviour. Is this a fact, an interpretation, or both? What would you need to support it?

objectives: I can follow the events from the rebellion to the ruin of the cities.
I can explain what “this situation” refers to.
I can tell the writer’s description from what “Sources say”.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Put five sentences in order using the linking words at their start, then match four expressions of destruction with their meanings (wiped out, leaving not a single stone standing, like a roller, hardly anyone remained there). The last activity asks you to explain why Kösedağ is more than a battlefield event.
content.pronunciationFocus: Names: KÖ-se-dağ, er-ZU-rum, SI-vas, KAY-se-ri, er-zin-JAN. Stress: sup-PRESSED, PLUN-dered, CAP-tive. Read the years twelve forty-two and twelve forty-three clearly.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Trap at Kösedağ”. What tactic did the Mongols use? Listen once. Paragraph 3 describes violence; read it calmly and focus on the order of events. Read again and underline the linking word at the start of each step.
discussionPoints: Yunus lived his whole life while this storm swept across Anatolia. What kind of words do people need from a poet in such a time?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Trap at Kösedağ” and “Cities in Ruins”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to the start of paragraph 2 and find “this situation”. Read the last sentence of paragraph 1. Check the year of Kösedağ: It came later. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Explain in five to six sentences why Kösedağ was a turning point. Link the battle to what came before and after it, and keep the most extreme claim attributed to the sources, as the chapter does with “Sources say:”.

whatToNotice: The linking words carry the story: In the end, However, In late 1242, Finally, Following their easy victory.
Notice “Sources say:” before the most extreme sentence. The writer attributes it to historical sources instead of presenting it as his own measurement.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Trap at Kösedağ”. What tactic did the Mongols use?
Listen once. Paragraph 3 describes violence; read it calmly and focus on the order of events.
Read again and underline the linking word at the start of each step.
Open the picture hotspots “Trap at Kösedağ” and “Cities in Ruins” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find how the rebellion ended and how difficult it was.
Paragraph 2: find what the Mongols did in late 1242 and how the Seljuk people felt.
Paragraph 3: find the place and year of the battle, the tactic, and the three cities destroyed after it.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: false retreat, captive, suppressed, plundered, slaughtered.
“this Mongol storm swept across Anatolia like a roller, leaving behind blood, misery, and ruins.” What does the image of a roller add to the facts?
Write one sentence with suppressed and one with false retreat.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks what gave the Mongols courage. Read the first sentence of paragraph 2, then the end of paragraph 1 to see what “this situation” means.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to the start of paragraph 2 and find “this situation”.
Read the last sentence of paragraph 1.
Check the year of Kösedağ: It came later. Try again.
selfCheck: Can I retell the events in the right order?
Can I explain what “this situation” refers to?
Can I say why the last sentence begins with “Sources say:”?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Explain in five to six sentences why Kösedağ was a turning point. Link the battle to what came before and after it, and keep the most extreme claim attributed to the sources, as the chapter does with “Sources say:”.
content.reflectionPrompt: Yunus lived his whole life while this storm swept across Anatolia. What kind of words do people need from a poet in such a time?

objectives: I can trace the stages from agreement to dependency to direct rule.
I can explain a comparison introduced with “almost as if”.
I can praise an effort and still say it failed, using “Nevertheless”.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Choose what “almost as if they were” means (they kept their titles but behaved like officials), complete the stages with “in time”, “while”, “Nevertheless” and “Finally”, then turn noun phrases into clauses (“small principalities emerged”, “became poorer”). The last activity asks you to describe how an agreement became dependency and then direct attachment.
content.pronunciationFocus: Names: ce-la-led-DIN ka-ra-TAY, IL-kha-nate. Stress: prin-CI-pal-i-ties, de-PEN-dent, CON-flict. Read the year thirteen oh eight clearly, and pause after “Nevertheless,”.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Sultans as Officials”. Were the sultans really officials? Listen once and follow the stages. Read paragraphs 2 and 3 again and circle “In the end”, “in time”, “However”, “Nevertheless” and “Finally”.
discussionPoints: Karatay tried to bring some relief to the people, even though it was not enough. Is an effort worth making when you know it may not succeed?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Sultans as Officials” and “Ilkhanate Empire”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 3. Read what the efforts aimed at, then read “Nevertheless, these efforts were not enough.” Check what happened in 1308, then decide again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Describe the stages from the agreement to 1308 in five to six sentences. Use “In the end”, “in time”, “Nevertheless” and “Finally”, and turn at least one noun phrase into a clause.

whatToNotice: The chapter is a process: small principalities, panic, an agreement, dependency, a growing tax, poverty, and finally direct attachment in 1308.
Notice “The Seljuk sultans began to act almost as if they were Mongols’ civil officials.” “as if” and “almost” mark a comparison, not a literal fact.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Sultans as Officials”. Were the sultans really officials?
Listen once and follow the stages.
Read paragraphs 2 and 3 again and circle “In the end”, “in time”, “However”, “Nevertheless” and “Finally”.
Open the picture hotspots “Sultans as Officials” and “Ilkhanate Empire” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find what the weakening of the Seljuks led to and what the principalities fought over.
Paragraph 2: find what was sent to the Mongols and what the growing tax did.
Paragraph 3: find what Jalal al-Din Karatay tried to do and what happened in 1308.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: dependent state, relief, principalities, conflict, attached.
“Nevertheless, these efforts were not enough.” How does Nevertheless respect the efforts and still judge them?
Write one sentence with dependent state and one with relief.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The statement is about what statesmen like Karatay achieved. Read the last paragraph, especially the sentence with “Nevertheless” and the one with 1308.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 3.
Read what the efforts aimed at, then read “Nevertheless, these efforts were not enough.”
Check what happened in 1308, then decide again.
selfCheck: Can I list the stages in order?
Can I explain “almost as if they were Mongols’ civil officials”?
Can I explain why “Therefore” would be wrong instead of “Nevertheless”?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Describe the stages from the agreement to 1308 in five to six sentences. Use “In the end”, “in time”, “Nevertheless” and “Finally”, and turn at least one noun phrase into a clause.
content.reflectionPrompt: Karatay tried to bring some relief to the people, even though it was not enough. Is an effort worth making when you know it may not succeed?

content.chapter: Chapter 7: Yunus Appears as a Wise Dervish
objectives: I can explain how the chaos in Anatolia shaped Yunus’s response.
I can notice a careful verb (“tried”) that limits a claim.
I can name the sources of Yunus’s understanding of Sufism.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Match five phrases with their meaning (under Mongol pressure, During the same period, were dominant among nomads, through the lens of, using poetry as his medium), then join ideas with “and he used”, “who” and “because the Mongols pressured them”. The last activity asks you to write 5–7 sentences on how the chapter moves from crisis to Yunus’s response.
content.pronunciationFocus: Names: TUR-kes-tan, trans-OX-i-a-na, kho-ra-SAN, KHWA-rezm. Stress: DER-vish-es, ME-di-um, FAITH-ful-ness. Read the list of regions with a small pause at each comma.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Poetry as a Medium”. What is a medium? Listen once for the situation, the response and the sources. Read paragraph 2 again and mark the verb that describes what Yunus did.
discussionPoints: Yunus tried to help people make sense of life in hard days. What helps you make sense of a hard time: People, words, faith, or something else?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Popular Sufism” and “Poetry as a Medium”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 2. Find the verb after “He” and ask whether the writer says he succeeded. Check paragraph 1: the shaykhs from Khorasan are a different group. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write 5–7 sentences that move from the crisis to Yunus’s response. Use “under … pressure”, “During the same period”, “through the lens of” and a participle phrase with using.

whatToNotice: The chapter moves from context (chaos, shaykhs, dervishes) to Yunus’s response and then to the sources of his thought.
Notice “He tried to respond to people’s efforts to make sense of life in hard days”. “Tried” describes a response, not a solution; the chapter does not claim his poems ended the chaos.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Poetry as a Medium”. What is a medium?
Listen once for the situation, the response and the sources.
Read paragraph 2 again and mark the verb that describes what Yunus did.
Open the picture hotspots “Popular Sufism” and “Poetry as a Medium” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find where the shaykhs came from, why they came and what their dervishes spread.
Paragraph 2: find how Yunus responded and what he used as his medium.
Paragraph 3: find the sources of his understanding of Sufism and what his poems express.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: medium, faithfulness, chaos, dervishes, lens.
“through the lens of his Sufi identity”. Why does the writer use the image of a lens?
Write one sentence with medium and one with lens.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks how the writer describes Yunus’s response. Paragraph 2 gives it in one long sentence; notice the first verb.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 2.
Find the verb after “He” and ask whether the writer says he succeeded.
Check paragraph 1: the shaykhs from Khorasan are a different group. Try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain the context of Yunus’s response?
Can I explain why “tried” matters?
Can I name three sources of his Sufism?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write 5–7 sentences that move from the crisis to Yunus’s response. Use “under … pressure”, “During the same period”, “through the lens of” and a participle phrase with using.
content.reflectionPrompt: Yunus tried to help people make sense of life in hard days. What helps you make sense of a hard time: People, words, faith, or something else?

objectives: I can explain tawhid and the Unity of Existence as the chapter presents them.
I can tell whose view an idea belongs to.
I can separate a cause from a result in an abstract argument.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Choose why the writer begins with “According to …” (to show whose view or theory the idea belongs to), then choose the links “From this perspective”, “for this reason” and “Nonetheless”. The last activity asks you to explain the connection between tawhid, true reality and creation with careful attribution.
content.pronunciationFocus: Words: taw-HEED, vah-DET-i vü-JUT. Stress: AB-so-lute, man-i-fes-TA-tions, dis-IN-te-grat-ed, per-SPEC-tive. Read the verse in two parts, with a pause after “Tawhid;”.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Source of All Things”. What follows from the idea that Allah is the source of all things? Listen once. Read the verse slowly and notice who knows Tawhid. Read again and mark “therefore”, “From this perspective”, “for this reason”, “As a result of” and “Nonetheless”.
discussionPoints: “Whoever denies this Tawhid is an enemy to his own soul.” Why might Yunus see denial as a harm to oneself rather than to others?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Unity of Existence” and “Source of All Things”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Find “for this reason” at the end of paragraph 1: what comes before it is the reason. Find “As a result of creation” in the last paragraph: What comes after it is a result. Decide which came first, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Explain in five to six sentences how tawhid, true reality and creation are connected. Attribute every idea with “According to Yunus Emre” or “According to the theory”, and keep cause and result in the right order.

whatToNotice: The chapter builds an argument in steps: Tawhid, Allah as the source of all things, the Unity of Existence, creation, and multiple existence.

Notice “According to Yunus Emre” and “According to the theory of the Unity of Existence”. These phrases attribute ideas to a person and to a school of thought; when the writer quotes Yunus, the frame changes to “Yunus says:”.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Source of All Things”. What follows from the idea that Allah is the source of all things?
Listen once. Read the verse slowly and notice who knows Tawhid.
Read again and mark “therefore”, “From this perspective”, “for this reason”, “As a result of” and “Nonetheless”.
Open the picture hotspots “Unity of Existence” and “Source of All Things” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find the meaning of tawhid and why everything is connected to Allah.
Paragraph 1: find why, according to the theory, Allah created the worlds.
The verse and the last paragraph: Find what the verse says about Adam and what happened as a result of creation.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: absolute, manifestations, disintegrated, perspective, attributes.
“this multiple existence is nothing but manifestations of the names of Allah.” What does “nothing but” add?
Write one sentence with perspective and one with disintegrated.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The statement joins the reason for creation and the breaking of unity. Compare the end of paragraph 1 with the last paragraph of the chapter.
wrongAnswerSupport: Find “for this reason” at the end of paragraph 1: what comes before it is the reason.
Find “As a result of creation” in the last paragraph: What comes after it is a result.
Decide which came first, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain what tawhid means?
Can I say why the writer uses “According to …”?
Can I explain what “Nonetheless” keeps together?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Explain in five to six sentences how tawhid, true reality and creation are connected. Attribute every idea with “According to Yunus Emre” or “According to the theory”, and keep cause and result in the right order.
content.reflectionPrompt: “Whoever denies this Tawhid is an enemy to his own soul.” Why might Yunus see denial as a harm to oneself rather than to others?

objectives: I can explain how love and unity are connected in Yunus’s thought.
I can tell a purpose, a conclusion and a reason apart in an argument.
I can connect an idea with a religious practice.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Sort six sentences into a goal, a conclusion from the ideas before, or a reason (“For, according to him, …”), then complete the fixed expressions “stands out”, “lies at the core of” and “extends to”. The last activity asks you to explain how the chapter moves from “everything which is created is a reflection” to love, harmony and religious practice.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: HAR-mo-ny, re-FLEC-tion, foun-DA-tion, in-ter-re-LAT-ed. Read the “Therefore” sentence as two mirror halves: the CRE-a-tor / the cre-AT-ed, the cre-AT-ed / the CRE-a-tor.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Love Brings Unity”. What does love bring? Listen once for the goal of humanity and the goal of love. Read again and mark “In this sense”, “Therefore”, “From this perspective” and “For, according to him”.
discussionPoints: Yunus says that where love is absent, anger, heartbreak and separation arise. Where have you seen this happen, and what brought people together again?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Love Brings Unity” and “The Five Daily Prayers”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Take one item at a time. Find the part of the chapter where it appears: first paragraph, verse, or the paragraphs on love. Match again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write five to six sentences that connect the chapter’s ideas: reflection, unity, the five daily prayers, love and harmony. Use at least one purpose phrase, one conclusion signal and one reason with “For”.

whatToNotice: The chapter moves from reality (everything is a reflection) to practice (Allah’s commands and the five daily prayers) and then to love.
Notice “Therefore, those who love the Creator love the created, and those who love the created also love the Creator.” The two halves mirror each other to show a two-way link.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Love Brings Unity”. What does love bring?
Listen once for the goal of humanity and the goal of love.
Read again and mark “In this sense”, “Therefore”, “From this perspective” and “For, according to him”.
Open the picture hotspots “Love Brings Unity” and “The Five Daily Prayers” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: The opening paragraph: Find what everything created is and what the ultimate purpose of humanity is.
The verse: Find what anyone who claims to be a Muslim should do.
The last two paragraphs: Find where love lies in his philosophy and what arises where love is absent.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: harmony, core, reflection, foundation, interrelated.
“Love for the created is an extension of the love of Allah.” How does this sentence prepare the “Therefore” sentence after it?
Write one sentence with harmony and one with interrelated.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will match four ideas with what the chapter says. The first paragraph is about creation, the verse is about worship, and the last two paragraphs are about love.
wrongAnswerSupport: Take one item at a time.
Find the part of the chapter where it appears: first paragraph, verse, or the paragraphs on love.
Match again.
selfCheck: Can I explain the ultimate purpose of humanity in the chapter?
Can I explain the two-way link in the “Therefore” sentence?
Can I say what “For” means at the start of a sentence?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write five to six sentences that connect the chapter’s ideas: reflection, unity, the five daily prayers, love and harmony. Use at least one purpose phrase, one conclusion signal and one reason with “For”.
content.reflectionPrompt: Yunus says that where love is absent, anger, heartbreak and separation arise. Where have you seen this happen, and what brought people together again?

objectives: I can explain the heart metaphor and its moral consequence.
I can describe the three types of intellect.
I can separate a metaphor from a literal claim.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Match the practical reason, the limited intellect, the universal intellect and “a light from Allah that has existed since eternity” with their meanings, then correct three forms: “are the values”, “the place where” and “described … as”. The last activity asks you to explain the heart metaphor and one moral consequence without treating it as a literal claim about the body.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: IN-tel-lect, e-TER-ni-ty, PI-e-ty, PU-ri-ty, per-CEIVES. Read the verse slowly, with a pause after “the Lord,” and after “the heart.”.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Throne of the Lord”. What does the phrase mean in the chapter? Listen once for the heart and then for the intellect. Read the last paragraph again and mark the three types of intellect with their relative clauses.
discussionPoints: Yunus warns that whoever destroys a heart is the most unfortunate of the two worlds. How can words break a heart, and how can they mend one?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Throne of the Lord” and “Light from Allah”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to the paragraph before the verse. Read what the heart is called just before “For this reason”. Choose the option that gives that reason, not another idea from the book. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Explain the heart metaphor in five to six sentences. Clarify it with “that is”, draw one moral consequence with “For this reason”, and make clear that it is a metaphor, not a claim about the body.

whatToNotice: The chapter gives value to both the heart and the intellect; it does not set one against the other.
Notice “For this reason, he described breaking a heart as destroying Allah’s house.” The metaphor of the throne leads directly to a moral warning.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Throne of the Lord”. What does the phrase mean in the chapter?
Listen once for the heart and then for the intellect.
Read the last paragraph again and mark the three types of intellect with their relative clauses.
Open the picture hotspots “Throne of the Lord” and “Light from Allah” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: The paragraph before the verse: Find what the heart is the center of and why breaking a heart is serious.
The paragraph after the verse: Find why purity of the heart matters and what the heart perceives.
The last paragraph: Find how Yunus describes intellect and what each of the three types does.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: piety, intellect, eternity, purity, perceives.
“the heart is the eye that perceives the truth and the center of understanding.” Is this a literal or a figurative description? How do you know?
Write one sentence with purity and one with piety.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why breaking a heart is described as destroying Allah’s house. Find “For this reason” in the paragraph before the verse and read the sentence just before it.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to the paragraph before the verse.
Read what the heart is called just before “For this reason”.
Choose the option that gives that reason, not another idea from the book. Try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain the throne metaphor?
Can I describe the three types of intellect?
Can I correct “described breaking a heart like destroying”?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Explain the heart metaphor in five to six sentences. Clarify it with “that is”, draw one moral consequence with “For this reason”, and make clear that it is a metaphor, not a claim about the body.
content.reflectionPrompt: Yunus warns that whoever destroys a heart is the most unfortunate of the two worlds. How can words break a heart, and how can they mend one?

objectives: I can explain why heart and reason must support one another.
I can identify the evidence the writer gives for a claim.
I can tell the different meanings of must and may.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Sort lines by what “must” or “may” expresses (a necessary condition, something certain for everyone, a wish or prayer), then rewrite with “so that”, “no better advisor than death” and “the role of death as an advisor”. The last activity asks you to explain how awareness of death works as an advisor in the chapter.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: sal-VA-tion, ad-VI-sor, ad-VI-so-ry, e-VEN-tu-al-ly, HOME-land. Read the hadith slowly and without adding words: “Those who remember death the most and prepare best for what comes after it are the wisest.”
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “The Best Advisor”. Who or what is the best advisor? Listen once. Read both verses slowly. Read again and mark every “must” and “May” and what each one expresses.
discussionPoints: A guest knows the visit will end. How might living like a guest change the way you use your time, your money and your words?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Heart and Reason Together” and “The Best Advisor”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to the paragraph between the verses. Read the claim, then what the writer adds straight after it. Check the reference in brackets, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Explain in five to six sentences how remembering death can guide a life. Use must for a necessary condition, keep the hadith exactly as the chapter gives it, and separate the guidance from any automatic result.

whatToNotice: The chapter has two themes, each followed by a verse: heart and reason, then death.
Notice “as the Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) said:”. The writer supports Yunus’s view with a hadith and gives its reference (Ibn Majah, Zuhd, 31, hadith 4259).
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “The Best Advisor”. Who or what is the best advisor?
Listen once. Read both verses slowly.
Read again and mark every “must” and “May” and what each one expresses.
Open the picture hotspots “Heart and Reason Together” and “The Best Advisor” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: The first paragraph: Find what heart and reason must do for a person to reach salvation.
The paragraph between the verses: Find Yunus’s view of death and the hadith that supports it.
The last verse: Find what a guest in this world must one day do.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: advisor, salvation, eventually, meaningful, homeland.
“A guest in this world, one day they must set out for their homeland”. What does homeland mean here, according to the Word Note?
Write one sentence with eventually and one with meaningful.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks what evidence supports the claim about the best advisor. Read the paragraph between the two verses to the end of the sentence with that claim.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to the paragraph between the verses.
Read the claim, then what the writer adds straight after it.
Check the reference in brackets, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain why heart and reason need each other?
Can I name the evidence for death as the best advisor?
Can I explain the two meanings of must in the chapter?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Explain in five to six sentences how remembering death can guide a life. Use must for a necessary condition, keep the hadith exactly as the chapter gives it, and separate the guidance from any automatic result.
content.reflectionPrompt: A guest knows the visit will end. How might living like a guest change the way you use your time, your money and your words?

objectives: I can explain Yunus’s definition of morality.
I can contrast virtues and harmful habits from the chapter.
I can explain what the images of the two verses mean.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Choose what “by addressing …” shows (the way he warned people), correct “consists of abandoning”, “are important” and “teaches”, then build “Yunus Emre’s poems are not only literary works but also a moral guide”. The last activity asks you to contrast two virtues with two harmful traits in one paragraph.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: hu-MIL-i-ty, an-i-mal-IS-tic, STIN-gi-ness, BACK-bit-ing, SLAN-der. Read the list of negative traits evenly, and stress not ONLY … but ALSO.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Harmful Habits”. How many habits does it list? Listen once for the definition, the two lists and the two verses. Read the first paragraph again and copy the values and the negative traits into two columns.
discussionPoints: Yunus warned against backbiting and slander. Why are these habits easy to fall into, and what helps you stay away from them?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Virtues to Keep” and “Harmful Habits”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the first two sentences of the chapter again. Find the key word of each verse: greed or patience. Match again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write a paragraph that contrasts two virtues with two harmful traits from the chapter. Explain what each does to a person, use one verse as support, and do not turn the paragraph into a list.

whatToNotice: The first paragraph gives a definition, two lists (values and negative traits) and a claim about the poems; the verses then give images for greed and patience.
Notice “Yunus Emre’s poems are not only literary works but also a moral guide.” This is the writer’s judgment, and it prepares the final chapter.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Harmful Habits”. How many habits does it list?
Listen once for the definition, the two lists and the two verses.
Read the first paragraph again and copy the values and the negative traits into two columns.
Open the picture hotspots “Virtues to Keep” and “Harmful Habits” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: The first paragraph: Find how morality is defined and how immoral behaviors are described.
The first paragraph: Find the seven values and how Yunus warned people about harmful habits.
The verses: Find the prison image and what those blessed with patience will achieve.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: humility, animalistic self, righteous life, negative traits, greed.
“I’ve fallen into the prison of greed and cannot escape”. Why is a prison a strong image for greed?
Write one sentence with humility and one with negative traits.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will match two definitions and two verses with their meanings. The first two sentences of the chapter give the definitions; each verse has one key word.
wrongAnswerSupport: Read the first two sentences of the chapter again.
Find the key word of each verse: greed or patience.
Match again.
selfCheck: Can I define morality as Yunus does?
Can I name three values and three harmful habits?
Can I correct “Values … is important”?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write a paragraph that contrasts two virtues with two harmful traits from the chapter. Explain what each does to a person, use one verse as support, and do not turn the paragraph into a list.
content.reflectionPrompt: Yunus warned against backbiting and slander. Why are these habits easy to fall into, and what helps you stay away from them?

objectives: I can explain what the last verses teach about patience, anger and arrogance.
I can recognize the writer’s confident stance.
I can write a conclusion that joins Yunus’s literary and moral legacy.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for the argument, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
content.grammarFocus: Match four lines of the verses with their meanings, then keep the writer’s certainty with a stance adverb such as “Clearly”, and rewrite the two-part claim with “in addition to being” and “both … and”. The last activity asks you to write a 6–8 sentence conclusion on why Yunus Emre remains significant.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: LEG-a-cy, PROM-i-nent, AR-ro-gance, pos-SESS-es. Read It is OB-vi-ous that … with firm, falling intonation, and give “not only” and “but also” equal weight.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, open the hotspot “Guide for Generations”. What are his writings valuable as? Listen once. Read each verse as a short rule for life. Read the last paragraph again and mark the two parts after “not only” and “but also”.
discussionPoints: Yunus says that whoever is filled with anger loses their faith. What does patience look like for you in a real moment of anger?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Patience and Anger” and “Guide for Generations”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to the last paragraph. Ask whether “It is obvious that” reports someone else’s view or shows the writer’s own certainty. Choose again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write a 6–8 sentence conclusion on why Yunus Emre remains significant. Use evidence from at least two earlier chapters, join his literary and moral legacy with “not only … but also”, and show your stance with one clear marker.

whatToNotice: The chapter gives two verses and then one final paragraph of judgment about the whole book.
Notice “It is obvious that Yunus Emre was not only a prominent figure in his own time but also left a lasting legacy.” “It is obvious that” shows the writer’s own strong certainty, not a report.
readListen: Before you read, open the hotspot “Guide for Generations”. What are his writings valuable as?
Listen once. Read each verse as a short rule for life.
Read the last paragraph again and mark the two parts after “not only” and “but also”.
Open the picture hotspots “Patience and Anger” and “Guide for Generations” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: The first verse: Find who rises to the heavens and what lies within patience.
The second verse: Find what anger does to faith and what one must give up.
The last paragraph: Find the two reasons his writings are valuable and for whom.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: legacy, prominent, arrogance, possesses, future generations.
“For within patience lies every kind of skill”. Why does the writer put “within patience” first?
Write one sentence with legacy and one with prominent about a person you admire.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks how the writer presents the claim about his legacy. Read the first words of the last paragraph.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to the last paragraph.
Ask whether “It is obvious that” reports someone else’s view or shows the writer’s own certainty.
Choose again.
selfCheck: Can I explain both verses in my own words?
Can I explain what “It is obvious that” shows?
Can I rewrite the claim with “both … and”?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write a 6–8 sentence conclusion on why Yunus Emre remains significant. Use evidence from at least two earlier chapters, join his literary and moral legacy with “not only … but also”, and show your stance with one clear marker.

metadata.title: Yunus Emre B2 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Read • Find • Judge • Build • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 30 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: B2 learners who study the life, times and poetry of Yunus Emre on their own or at home.
learningGoals: Understand the history and the ideas of the 13 chapters.
Find evidence in the story before answering.
Tell reports, verses and the hadith from the writer’s interpretation.
Use qualified language when the evidence is qualified.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in a short piece of your own.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Listen and read before the Quick Challenge.
Repair wrong answers with the text, not with guesses.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 13.

sections.title: 1. One Chapter per Session
sections.text: Each chapter takes about 30 minutes. Open “Study Path” for the steps of your chapter.
points: Preview the title and hotspots.
Listen and read for the argument.
Find the evidence.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 2. Listen and Read
sections.text: Use the audio twice: Once for the argument, once to follow the exact wording.
points: First listening: What is the writer claiming?
Second listening: Follow the text line by line.
Replay one long sentence or one verse and read it with the same pauses and stress.

sections.title: 3. Evidence or Interpretation?
sections.text: This book mixes historical reports, Yunus Emre’s verses, a hadith and the writer’s own judgments. Learn to tell them apart.
points: A report keeps a distance: “According to historical accounts”, “Some sources note that”, “Sources say:”.
A verse is introduced with “Yunus says:”, and the hadith in Chapter 11 has a reference in brackets.
An idea can belong to a person or a theory: “According to Yunus Emre”, “In his view”.
A judgment evaluates: “even worsened”, “almost as if”, “It is obvious that”. Keep your own claims as careful as the evidence.

sections.title: 4. Word Notes and Hotspots
sections.text: Each chapter has five Word Notes and two picture hotspots. Use them after you have tried to work out the meaning yourself.
points: Guess the meaning from the sentence.
Check the Word Note.
Use the word in a sentence that explains a cause, a contrast or a value.

sections.title: 5. Quick Challenge and Language Focus
sections.text: Answer the Quick Challenge before reading the feedback. Then do the three or four Language Focus activities.
points: First activity (Notice): See what a word or sentence does in the argument.
Middle activities (Build): sort, match, choose, correct or rewrite forms from the chapter.
Last activity (Use): Write a short B2 response of your own.

sections.title: 6. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Work one paragraph or one verse at a time.
Write a one-line summary of each paragraph.
Mark reports, verses and the writer’s judgments in three colors.
Focus on two Word Notes today.

sections.title: 7. Values in the Story
sections.text: Yunus Emre’s poems are a moral guide as well as literature. Connect each value to one action.
points: Generosity and detachment: Give without expecting a return, and do not hold on to wealth, status and fame (Chapters 1, 11).
Love for all: Those who love the Creator love the created (Chapter 9).
Respect for every heart: Breaking a heart is like destroying Allah’s house (Chapter 10).
Humility and patience: Leave arrogance and anger behind (Chapters 12, 13).
Clear words in hard times: speak to people in a language they understand (Chapters 1, 7).

sections.title: 8. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 13, do the review pages in this order. Go back to the chapter when an answer is not clear.
